title: Machine Learning × Deep Learning: A MECE Knowledge Tree of Algorithms
criterion: L1 split criterion: Where does the learning signal come from?
criterionDetail: Every learning algorithm optimizes some objective, and the "signal" that objective needs can come from only four sources: externally provided labels, rewards obtained by interacting with an environment, or no external signal at all. Without an external signal, there are only two options: describe the structure of the data itself (unsupervised), or construct a proxy prediction task from the data (self-supervised). The four branches are therefore mutually exclusive by definition and collectively exhaustive by logic.

levels.name: Learning Paradigm
levels.rule: Source of the learning signal (external labels / data structure / self-constructed proxy objective / environment reward)

levels.name: Problem Type
levels.rule: Each paradigm uses a single criterion of its own: supervised by "dependency topology of the inputs", unsupervised by "type of output", self-supervised by "how the proxy objective is constructed", and reinforcement learning by "whether decisions change the environment's state"

levels.name: Mathematical Philosophy / Model Family
levels.rule: Within one problem type, split by "hypothesis space and inductive bias", e.g. linear boundaries, the kernel trick, tree ensembles, attention, diffusion

levels.name: Specific Algorithm
levels.rule: The representative algorithm itself; each algorithm appears exactly once, placed according to its "most typical training objective, as demonstrated in the original paper"

notation: Sequence length or number of time steps
Number of layers or tokens (depending on context)
Number of trees or weak learners

Number of nodes and edges in a graph

boundaries.q: Why doesn't the supervised L2 split simply use "regression / classification"?
boundaries.a: Regression vs. classification is an "output type", and the same algorithm (XGBoost, random forest, KNN, MLP) can usually do both. Splitting on it would place the same L4 in two branches, violating mutual exclusivity. Splitting instead on "the dependency topology among input elements" (unstructured / 1D sequence / regular grid / arbitrary graph) gives every algorithm exactly one home, while regression/classification is shown as a tag on each algorithm.

boundaries.q: PCA and autoencoders both reconstruct data, so why is one unsupervised and the other self-supervised?
boundaries.a: The test is what is produced and how it is trained: PCA solves directly for the variance structure of the data via eigendecomposition, and what it produces is "a description of this particular dataset" (coordinates); an autoencoder uses gradient-based training to fit a reusable parametric network that performs the proxy task of "reconstruction". Under squared error, the optimal subspace of a linear autoencoder coincides with that of PCA, which is exactly where the two branches meet.

boundaries.q: GMM, KDE and VAE all model p(x). How are they told apart?
boundaries.a: GMM is mainly used to partition samples into clusters (output: cluster labels) → unsupervised / clustering; KDE is used to assess the density or rarity of each point (output: density scores) → unsupervised / density & anomaly; VAE learns a generative mapping from the prior N(0,I) to the data, used to sample new data → self-supervised / generative.

boundaries.q: GPT generates content, so why is it under "predictive" rather than "generative"?
boundaries.a: The L2 criterion is "how the proxy objective is constructed", not "whether it can generate". GPT's training objective is to predict the next token from the preceding context in data space (a chain-rule factorization into conditional likelihoods), with no transformation starting from noise or a latent prior; the objectives of diffusion, flow models, GANs and VAEs, by contrast, learn a "prior → data distribution" mapping.

boundaries.q: Why does the Transformer appear in different branches of the tree?
boundaries.a: Each L4 is an "architecture × training objective" combination, not merely an architecture name. The original encoder-decoder Transformer was trained on supervised translation (supervised / sequence); GPT and BERT are self-supervised pretraining (self-supervised / predictive); ViT was introduced for supervised image classification (supervised / grid); DiT is a backbone for a diffusion objective (self-supervised / generative). Same architecture, different learning problems, so there is no duplication.

boundaries.q: DPO never interacts with an environment, so why is it classified under reinforcement learning?
boundaries.a: DPO's derivation starts from KL-regularized reward maximization (the RL objective of RLHF) and its output is a policy; it merely uses a closed-form solution to turn the RL problem into a classification loss over preference pairs. It "solves an RL objective with a supervised loss", and is placed under policy-based methods according to the objective it optimizes.

boundaries.q: HMMs can be trained with or without supervision. Where do they belong?
boundaries.a: By their most typical use, "sequence labeling and segmentation", they are placed under supervised / 1D sequence / probabilistic graphical sequence models, and the card notes that they can be trained unsupervised with Baum-Welch (EM).

boundaries.q: CLIP uses image-text pairs. Does that count as supervised?
boundaries.a: The paired text is a signal that occurs naturally on the web and was never manually annotated for a specific task; CLIP uses it to build a "matched vs. unmatched" contrastive objective and learn general-purpose representations, so it is placed under self-supervised / joint-embedding. The literature also calls this "natural language supervision" or weak supervision.

hybrids: Supervised loss (few labels) + a self-supervised or unsupervised consistency objective (abundant unlabeled data), e.g. Pseudo-Label, FixMatch.
Supervised reward model (human preferences) + reinforcement-learning policy optimization (PPO).
First obtain representations via self-supervised pretraining, then fine-tune with a supervised objective; a pipeline rather than a new learning signal.
A form of supervised learning in which the labels are replaced by the teacher model's soft probability distribution.
Supervised learning + the model decides which sample to label next (the exploration strategy resembles a bandit).

children.name: Supervised Learning
children.signal: Externally provided target labels y: every training sample comes with an answer, either human-annotated or a historical outcome, and the model learns the mapping f: X → Y.
children.criterion: L2 split criterion: dependency topology among input elements (which determines the inductive bias the model should have)

children.name: Unstructured Feature Vectors (Tabular Data)
children.def: Each sample is a set of features with no fixed order or adjacency among them (columns can be permuted freely). The task can be regression or classification.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the mathematical philosophy of the hypothesis space (what the function looks like and how its complexity is controlled)

children.name: Regularized Linear Models
children.philosophy: Assumes a linear relationship between the target and the features (or a linear one after a link function), and controls complexity with a norm penalty to trade off bias against variance.

leaves.name: Ridge Regression
leaves.plain: Ordinary linear regression trusts the data too much: when features are very similar to one another, the coefficients swing wildly. Ridge attaches a rubber band to each coefficient that pulls it toward 0, reining them all in so none gets out of hand, and the model settles down. Every feature stays in the model; its influence is just discounted.
leaves.intuition: Adds an L2 penalty on the coefficients to least squares, shrinking them toward 0 without ever making them exactly 0. Equivalent to MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on the coefficients. When features are highly collinear, XᵀX has very small eigenvalues and its inverse is unstable; adding λI effectively "props up" those eigenvalues, so the solution becomes stable.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{\beta}\ \lVert y - X\beta \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \beta \rVert_2^2$
Closed-form solution: $\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y$

complexity.train: $O(nd^2 + d^3)$ (closed form); iterative methods $O(I \cdot n \cdot d)$

pros: Interpretable coefficients; well suited as a baseline model
use: Econometric or marketing mix models (MMM) with many collinear features
High-dimensional problems where most features contribute a little
The first baseline for any tabular task
cons: No feature selection: coefficients never become 0
Captures only linear relationships; interactions must be built by hand
Sensitive to feature scale; standardize first
Squared loss is sensitive to outliers
hp: Search 1e-4 to 1e3 on a log scale; RidgeCV offers efficient leave-one-out cross-validation
Required; otherwise the penalty treats features on different scales unfairly
The intercept should not be penalized (this is the default)

leaves.name: Lasso
leaves.zh: Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (L1 regularization)
leaves.plain: Like Ridge, it pulls coefficients toward 0, but much harder: unimportant features are set straight to zero and dropped from the model. So it predicts and picks features at the same time, leaving you with a short list of the variables that matter.
leaves.intuition: The contours of the L1 penalty are diamonds, and the loss contours tend to touch a diamond at one of its corners, which sit on the coordinate axes, so some coefficients come out exactly 0. Estimation and feature selection therefore happen in a single step. Equivalent to MAP estimation with a Laplace prior.
leaves.objective: $\min_{\beta}\ \frac{1}{2n} \lVert y - X\beta \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \beta \rVert_1$

complexity.train: Coordinate descent $O(I \cdot n \cdot d)$; full LARS path $O(n \cdot d \cdot \min(n, d))$
complexity.infer: $O(d)$ (in practice only the nonzero coefficients are used)

pros: Automatic feature selection yields a sparse, interpretable model
Still usable on high-dimensional data with d ≫ n
The regularization path gives an intuitive view of the order in which variables enter
use: Screening key drivers from a large pool of candidate variables
When a compact, interpretable scoring model is needed
Problems where the signal itself is sparse
cons: From a group of highly correlated features it picks just one, essentially at random, and the selection is unstable
When d > n it can select at most n features
Coefficients are systematically underestimated (shrinkage bias); fix with relaxed lasso or by refitting OLS on the selected variables
p-values after selection require dedicated post-selection inference methods
hp: Search along the regularization path with LassoCV; the 1-SE rule is commonly used to pick a sparser model
Increase max_iter if you get convergence warnings

leaves.name: ElasticNet
leaves.plain: A blend of Ridge and Lasso. Faced with a group of very similar features, Lasso often keeps just one at random; ElasticNet lets similar features enter or leave the model together, so it can still pick variables while staying more stable on collinear data.
leaves.intuition: Mixes L1 and L2: L1 makes the coefficients sparse, while L2 makes highly correlated features enter and leave the model as a group (the grouping effect), fixing Lasso's instability with collinear features. Think of it as Ridge-style decorrelation followed by Lasso-style selection.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{\beta}\ \frac{1}{2n} \lVert y - X\beta \rVert_2^2$
$\quad + \lambda \left[ \rho \lVert \beta \rVert_1 + \frac{1 - \rho}{2} \lVert \beta \rVert_2^2 \right]$
scikit-learn parameters: alpha = $\lambda$, l1_ratio = $\rho$

complexity.train: Coordinate descent $O(I \cdot n \cdot d)$

pros: Correlated features are selected as a group
Can select more than n features when d ≫ n
use: High-dimensional data with groups of correlated features, such as genomics, text n-grams and financial factors
An alternative when Lasso results are unstable
cons: Two hyperparameters must be tuned jointly
Still a linear model
Double shrinkage makes the coefficient bias larger (the original paper proposes rescaling by (1+λ₂) to correct it)
hp: Try [0.1, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 1]; the closer to 1, the more Lasso-like
ElasticNetCV can search alpha and l1_ratio together

leaves.name: Logistic Regression
leaves.plain: It gives each case a weighted score based on its features, then squashes that score into a probability between 0 and 1, e.g. "this customer has a 73% chance of churning." Simple, fast and easy to interpret (each coefficient tells you how much a feature pushes the probability up or down), it is the standard first move for any classification problem.
leaves.intuition: Passes the linear score wᵀx through a sigmoid to turn it into a probability, which is equivalent to assuming the log-odds are linear in the features. Maximizing the likelihood is the same as minimizing cross-entropy, which is convex, so finding the global optimum is guaranteed. For multiclass problems, use softmax instead.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{w}\ -\sum_{i} \big[\, y_i \log \sigma(w^\top x_i)$
$\quad + (1 - y_i) \log\big(1 - \sigma(w^\top x_i)\big) \big] + \lambda R(w)$
$\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$

complexity.train: $O(I \cdot n \cdot d)$ (iterative methods such as L-BFGS and SAG)

pros: Output probabilities are usually well calibrated
Coefficients can be read as odds ratios
Fast and robust; supports online learning
use: A strong baseline for any classification task
cons: Can only draw linear decision boundaries
Coefficients diverge when the data are perfectly separable; regularization is required
Class imbalance calls for adjusting class weights or the decision threshold
Performance depends heavily on feature engineering
hp: Smaller means stronger regularization; search on a log scale
l2 (default), l1 (requires liblinear or saga), elasticnet (requires saga)
lbfgs is the default; use saga for large or sparse data

children.name: Kernel Methods and Maximum Margin
children.philosophy: Uses a kernel function k(x, x′) = ⟨φ(x), φ(x′)⟩ to find a linear solution in a high- or even infinite-dimensional feature space without computing φ explicitly (the kernel trick); the solution depends only on similarities between samples.

leaves.name: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
leaves.plain: It draws a dividing line between two groups of points and keeps that line as far as possible from the nearest points on either side, like building the widest possible road between two crowds. The boundary is set only by the few points right at the roadside; with a kernel function, the road can curve too.
leaves.intuition: Among all hyperplanes that separate the two classes, pick the one with the largest margin: the larger the margin, the tighter the upper bound on generalization error. In the end only the points on the margin or violating it (the support vectors) determine the solution. Combined with the kernel trick, it yields nonlinear boundaries.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2$
$\quad + C \sum_{i} \max\big(0,\ 1 - y_i (w^\top \phi(x_i) + b)\big)$
(hinge loss; the dual problem involves only the kernel matrix $K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)$)

complexity.train: $O(n^2 d)$ to $O(n^3)$ (SMO in practice falls roughly in between)

pros: Generalizes well on small-to-medium, high-dimensional data
Convex optimization with a unique solution
Domain knowledge can be injected through the kernel
use: Classifier on top of pretrained features
cons: Training becomes very slow once n exceeds about 10⁵
Does not output probabilities directly (Platt scaling requires extra cross-validation)
Sensitive to feature scale and kernel parameters
Multiclass requires combining binary models via OvR or OvO
hp: Larger values approach a hard margin and overfit more easily; search 1e-2 to 1e3 on a log scale
Larger values make the decision boundary more curved; grid-search 1e-4 to 1e1 jointly with C
linear for high-dimensional sparse data (text); rbf in general

leaves.name: Support Vector Regression (SVR)
leaves.plain: The regression version of SVM. It allows an error tolerance band: as long as a prediction lands within a small range above or below the true value, it does not count as a miss, and only points outside that band are penalized. That makes it insensitive to small noise.
leaves.intuition: Carries the SVM margin idea over to regression: prediction errors inside an ε-wide "tube" cost nothing, and only points outside the tube are penalized. It is therefore insensitive to small noise, and the solution again depends only on the support vectors.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert w \rVert^2$
$\quad + C \sum_{i} \max\big(0,\ \lvert y_i - f(x_i) \rvert - \varepsilon\big)$
($\varepsilon$-insensitive loss)
pros: Linear (rather than squared) penalty makes it more robust to outliers
cons: Very slow on large data
Three hyperparameters (C, ε, γ) must be tuned jointly
No uncertainty estimates
hp: Set according to the target's scale, roughly on the order of the noise standard deviation
Standardizing the target is also recommended, so epsilon is easier to set

leaves.name: Gaussian Process Regression
leaves.plain: Instead of assuming up front what the function looks like, it only says "similar inputs should give similar outputs" and lets the data shape the rest. Its standout feature is that it tells you both the prediction and how uncertain it is: confident where data are plentiful, and honest about the uncertainty where data are scarce.
leaves.intuition: Rather than learning a set of parameters, it puts a prior directly on the function itself: the function values at any finite set of points follow a multivariate normal distribution whose covariance is set by the kernel. After observing data, Bayes' theorem gives the posterior, which provides both the predictive mean and its uncertainty (a confidence band).
leaves.objective:
Posterior mean: $\mu(x_*) = k_*^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y$
Hyperparameters: maximize the log marginal likelihood
$\log p(y \mid X, \theta) = -\tfrac{1}{2} y^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y$
$\quad - \tfrac{1}{2} \log \lvert K + \sigma^2 I \rvert - \tfrac{n}{2} \log 2\pi$

complexity.train: $O(n^3)$ (Cholesky decomposition)

pros: Kernels can encode prior knowledge such as smoothness and periodicity
cons: The O(n³) cost means approximations (sparse GPs, inducing points) are needed once n exceeds about 10⁴
Performance degrades with high-dimensional inputs
Kernel choice matters a lot
hp: RBF, Matern (ν = 2.5 is common), periodic; combine by adding or multiplying
Optimized automatically via the marginal likelihood; n_restarts_optimizer ≥ 5 recommended

children.name: Single Decision Trees and Bagging Ensembles
children.philosophy: Recursive binary splits partition the feature space into rectangular regions, each assigned a constant prediction; many mutually decorrelated trees are then trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and averaged to reduce variance.

leaves.name: CART Decision Tree
leaves.zh: Classification and regression tree (binary recursive partitioning)
leaves.plain: Like playing "20 Questions": at each step it picks the question that best separates the data (e.g. "Age > 35?"), keeps asking, and ends up with a set of if-then rules. People can read it, but a single tree tends to memorize the answers (overfitting).
leaves.intuition: At each step it greedily picks the feature and split point that most reduce the impurity of the child nodes (Gini or entropy for classification, squared error for regression), ending up with a readable set of if-then rules.
leaves.objective:
Each split maximizes $\Delta I = I(\text{parent}) - \frac{n_L}{n} I(L) - \frac{n_R}{n} I(R)$
$\text{Gini} = 1 - \sum_{k} p_k^2$
Cost-complexity pruning: $R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha \lvert T \rvert$

complexity.train: $O(d \cdot n \log n)$ (balanced tree, presorted features)

pros: Highly interpretable; converts directly into business rules
use: Rule extraction and communicating with the business
cons: High variance: a small change in the data can drastically change the tree structure
Only axis-parallel splits; diagonal boundaries need many splits
Greedy algorithm with no guarantee of a global optimum
Prone to overfitting
hp: The most effective regularizers; a min_samples_leaf of about 0.5–1% of the sample size is recommended

leaves.name: Random Forest
leaves.zh: Random forest (bagged trees with random feature subsets)
leaves.plain: It grows many decision trees, each seeing only part of the data and only some of the features at each split, so every tree has its own biases; then they vote or are averaged. It is like polling a panel of experts with different viewpoints: the average is more accurate and more stable than any one of them. On tabular data it works well with almost no tuning.
leaves.intuition: The variance of an average of B trees is ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B. Bootstrap sampling pushes down the second term, while choosing each split from only m randomly selected features lowers the correlation ρ between trees. That is why it beats plain bagging.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{y} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x)$
Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample; each split considers only $m$ randomly chosen features (classification $m \approx \sqrt{d}$, regression $m \approx d/3$)

complexity.train: $O(B \cdot m \cdot n \log n)$, fully parallelizable

pros: Works out of the box with little tuning
Resistant to overfitting; OOB error removes the need for cross-validation
Trains in parallel; robust to noise
use: A strong baseline for tabular data
cons: Large model; inference is slower than a single tree
Accuracy is usually slightly below that of well-tuned gradient-boosted trees
Impurity-based importance favors high-cardinality features (use permutation importance or SHAP instead)
Cannot extrapolate beyond the training range (a common weakness of tree models)
hp: 300–1000, until the OOB error stabilizes; more trees usually do not cause overfitting
Bootstrap sampling fraction for each tree

leaves.name: Extra Trees
leaves.plain: Even more laid-back than a random forest: instead of carefully searching for the best split point, it just picks one at random. Each tree is rougher, but the trees are less alike, so their average is actually more stable, and training is faster.
leaves.intuition: More random than a random forest: rather than searching for the best cut point, it draws one at random within each candidate feature's range, then picks the best of these random splits. It trades slightly higher bias for lower variance and faster training; no bootstrap by default.
leaves.objective:
Same averaged prediction as a random forest
Cut point $\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(\min\nolimits_j, \max\nolimits_j)$; among the $m$ candidate (feature, random cut point) pairs, take the one with the largest impurity decrease

complexity.train: $O(B \cdot m \cdot n \cdot \text{tree depth})$ (no sorting to find the best cut point, so smaller constants)

pros: Trains faster than a random forest
Lower variance and a smoother decision surface
use: A diversity-adding member of a stacked ensemble
cons: Slightly higher bias
May underperform a random forest when the signal is weak or there are few features
Models are just as large

children.name: Gradient Boosted Trees
children.philosophy: Gradient descent in function space: each new tree fits the negative gradient of the current model's loss (generalized residuals) and is added with a small step size. Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias.

leaves.name: GBDT
leaves.plain: It grows trees one after another, and each new tree focuses on fixing what all the previous trees still get wrong, like drilling only the questions you missed after an exam. After hundreds of these small corrections, predictions become very accurate; it is the prototype of the models that keep winning tabular-data competitions.
leaves.intuition: $F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu \cdot h_m(x)$, where $h_m$ fits the pseudo-residuals $r = -\partial L / \partial F$. Works with any differentiable loss (squared, absolute, Huber, log loss, quantile), generalizing AdaBoost into "gradient descent in function space."
leaves.objective:
Pseudo-residuals: $r_{im} = -\left[ \frac{\partial L(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)} \right]_{F = F_{m-1}}$
$h_m = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{h} \sum_{i} \big(r_{im} - h(x_i)\big)^2$
$F_m = F_{m-1} + \nu \cdot h_m$

complexity.train: $O(M \cdot d \cdot n \log n)$ (exact splits)

pros: Highly flexible choice of loss, enabling quantile and robust regression
The standard reference for understanding boosting
use: Scenarios that need a custom loss function
cons: Trees must be trained sequentially, one at a time, so it is much slower than XGBoost / LightGBM
Learning rate and number of trees must be tuned together
Sensitive to noisy labels
hp: 0.01–0.1; trades off inversely with n_estimators; use early stopping
For large data, switch to scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting

leaves.name: XGBoost
leaves.plain: An engineering-hardened version of GBDT. Besides correcting errors tree by tree, it has a built-in "don't grow overly complex trees" penalty to prevent overfitting, handles missing values and runs in parallel, so it is both accurate and fast. One of the top choices for tabular data.
leaves.intuition: Takes a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss and adds a tree-complexity penalty directly to the objective. This yields formulas for each leaf's optimal weight and for the split gain, turning "should we split further?" into a principled regularization decision. On the engineering side it adds sparsity-aware split finding, histogram approximation, caching and parallelization.
leaves.objective:
$\mathrm{Obj} = \sum_{i} l(y_i, \hat{y}_i) + \sum_{k} \Omega(f_k)$, $\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \tfrac{1}{2} \lambda \lVert w \rVert^2$
Optimal leaf weight: $w_j^* = -\frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}$
Split gain $= \tfrac{1}{2} \Big[ \frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}$
$\qquad - \frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda} \Big] - \gamma$
($G$ and $H$ are the sums of first- and second-order gradients over the node's samples)

complexity.train: Exact greedy: $O(M \cdot D \cdot \lVert x \rVert_0 \cdot \log n)$; the hist method needs about $O(nd)$ per tree to build histograms + $O(\text{bins} \cdot d \cdot \text{leaves})$

pros: A perennial winner in tabular-data competitions and in industry
Built-in regularization; learns a default branch direction for missing values
Supports GPU and distributed training, and custom losses
cons: Many hyperparameters that need tuning
High-cardinality categorical features must be encoded first
Cannot extrapolate
Hundreds of trees are hard to interpret as a whole; SHAP is needed
hp: Lower bound on the sum of Hessians in a leaf; prevents overly small leaves
L2 / L1 regularization on leaf weights

leaves.name: LightGBM
leaves.plain: Gradient-boosted trees sped up for big data. It bins numeric values into histograms, gives priority to the samples it gets most wrong, and bundles mutually exclusive sparse features together, so it trains much faster than XGBoost and uses less memory. The go-to choice when data volumes are large.
leaves.intuition: Two tricks designed for big data. GOSS keeps the samples with large gradients and only subsamples those with small gradients (reweighting them to compensate), cutting the number of samples; EFB bundles nearly mutually exclusive sparse features into one, cutting the number of features. Add leaf-wise growth, which always splits the leaf with the largest gain, and the loss drops further for the same number of leaves.
leaves.objective:
Same second-order objective as GBDT
Histogram binning, sped up by histogram subtraction: child histogram = parent − sibling

complexity.train: Building histograms is about $O(nd)$, and much less after GOSS / EFB; more than an order of magnitude faster than the exact method

pros: The top choice for a million samples or more
cons: Leaf-wise growth overfits easily on small data; limit num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf
Parameter names differ from XGBoost's, which is easy to confuse
More sensitive to hyperparameters
hp: The main complexity control; should be less than $2^{\texttt{max\_depth}}$, typically 31–255

leaves.name: CatBoost
leaves.plain: Gradient-boosted trees that excel at categorical features (city, product category, membership tier, and so on). It turns categories into numbers in a way that never peeks at the answer, avoiding information leakage, and usually performs very well with little tuning.
leaves.intuition: Solves boosting's "prediction shift": standard target encoding and gradient computation both use each sample's own label, causing target leakage. CatBoost instead uses an ordered scheme in which each sample's category statistics and residuals are computed only from the samples that precede it in a random permutation. It also uses symmetric (oblivious) trees: all nodes at the same level share the same split condition.
leaves.objective:
Ordered target statistics (categorical feature encoding):
$\hat{x}_i = \frac{\sum_{j<i,\ x_j = x_i} y_j + a \cdot P}{\sum_{j<i} \mathbf{1}[x_j = x_i] + a}$
Symmetric trees: all nodes at the same depth use the same (feature, threshold) pair

complexity.train: On the order of $O(M \cdot D \cdot n \cdot d)$, plus the extra overhead of maintaining multiple permutations
complexity.infer: $O(MD)$; symmetric trees can be evaluated with bit indexing, making it extremely fast

pros: The best native handling of categorical features among the three major GBDT libraries
Strong default parameters; resistant to overfitting
use: Business data with many categorical columns (region, product, channel)
Projects that need minimal tuning and a fast launch
cons: Usually trains slower than LightGBM on CPU
A single symmetric tree is less expressive
Larger model files
hp: Set automatically from the data by default
Cardinality threshold below which a categorical feature is one-hot encoded instead

children.name: Instance-Based Learning
children.philosophy: Builds no explicit model and treats the training data itself as the model; at prediction time, it takes a local vote or average under the smoothness assumption that "similar samples have similar outcomes".

leaves.name: k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
leaves.plain: "Birds of a feather flock together": to predict a new case, find the K existing cases most like it and see what most of them are, or what they average to. There is no training at all, but every prediction compares against all the data, so it gets slow as data grows, and features must be standardized first.
leaves.intuition: To predict a new point, find the k nearest training samples: take a majority vote for classification or the average for regression (optionally distance-weighted). Small k gives low bias and high variance; large k is smoother but more biased. At heart it is a nonparametric, local estimate of the conditional expectation.
leaves.objective:
Regression: $\hat{y}(x) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{N}_k(x)} y_i$
Classification: $\hat{y}(x) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{N}_k(x)} \mathbf{1}[y_i = c]$
The distance is typically $\lVert x - x_i \rVert_p$

complexity.train: $O(1)$; building a KD-tree / Ball-tree index takes $O(n \log n)$
complexity.infer: Brute force $O(nd)$ per query; about $O(\log n)$ with an index in low dimensions

pros: Can fit decision boundaries of any shape
cons: Curse of dimensionality: distances lose their discriminative power in high dimensions
Slow inference and a large memory footprint
Very sensitive to feature scale and irrelevant features
Dominated by the majority class when classes are imbalanced
hp: Search via cross-validation; on small data use an odd number to avoid ties
Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine (for text or embeddings)
Switch to approximate nearest-neighbor indexes such as FAISS or HNSW

children.name: Probabilistic Generative Classifiers
children.philosophy: First models "how each class generates data", p(x|y), together with the prior p(y), then inverts with Bayes' theorem to obtain p(y|x).

leaves.name: Naive Bayes
leaves.plain: It naively assumes every feature is independent of the others and simply multiplies together the evidence each clue provides to find the most likely class. Think of flagging an email as spam because it contains "you've won," "wire transfer" and "limited time." The assumption is unrealistic, but for text classification it is fast and surprisingly effective.
leaves.intuition: Assumes the features are conditionally independent given the class, so the joint likelihood factorizes into a product and each parameter needs only one-dimensional statistics. The assumption is almost always wrong, but classification only needs the classes to be ranked correctly, so in practice it often works surprisingly well.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{y} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c} \left[ \log P(c) + \sum_{j} \log P(x_j \mid c) \right]$
Multinomial NB (text): $P(w \mid c) = \frac{\operatorname{count}(w, c) + \alpha}{\sum_{w'} \operatorname{count}(w', c) + \alpha \lvert V \rvert}$

complexity.train: $O(nd)$

pros: Performs well on high-dimensional sparse text data
use: Baseline for text and sentiment classification
cons: The conditional-independence assumption leaves output probabilities badly miscalibrated (overconfident)
Correlated features get their votes counted more than once
The zero-frequency problem requires smoothing

leaves.name: Linear Discriminant Analysis
leaves.plain: It assumes each class's data looks like a cloud of the same shape, then finds a projection direction that spreads the different clouds as far apart as possible while packing points of the same class tightly together. It works both as a classifier and as a dimensionality-reduction tool.
leaves.intuition: Assumes each class is multivariate normal with a shared covariance matrix, so the log posterior ratio is linear in x, giving linear boundaries. Fisher's view is to find the projection direction that maximizes "between-class variance ÷ within-class variance," which is why LDA can also do supervised dimensionality reduction (to at most K − 1 dimensions).
leaves.objective:
Fisher criterion: $\max_{w}\ \frac{w^\top S_B w}{w^\top S_W w}$
Discriminant function: $\delta_c(x) = x^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mu_c - \tfrac{1}{2} \mu_c^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mu_c + \log \pi_c$
pros: Closed-form solution; stable on small samples
Doubles as supervised dimensionality reduction and visualization
cons: Requires normality and equal-covariance assumptions
Produces only linear boundaries
When d approaches n the covariance matrix becomes singular and shrinkage is needed
hp: At most K − 1 for dimensionality reduction
Switch to it when class covariances differ; gives quadratic boundaries (regularized via reg_param)

children.name: Neural Networks and Tabular Foundation Models
children.philosophy: Approximates arbitrary mappings with differentiable multilayer nonlinear functions (universal approximation theorem), optimized by backpropagation with stochastic gradient descent; recent extensions include pretrained tabular models that perform in-context learning directly at inference time.

leaves.name: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
leaves.plain: The most basic neural network: layers that each take a weighted sum and pass it through a nonlinear transformation, stacked one on top of another. In theory it can approximate any function. On tabular data it usually loses to gradient-boosted trees, but it is the basic building block of every deep learning model.
leaves.intuition: Each layer applies an affine transformation followed by a nonlinear activation, h = σ(Wx + b); stacking layers lets the network approximate any continuous function. Gradients are computed by backpropagation using the chain rule.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{\theta}\ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i} L(y_i, f_\theta(x_i)) + \lambda \lVert \theta \rVert^2$
$f_\theta(x) = W_L\, \sigma\big(\cdots \sigma(W_1 x + b_1) \cdots\big) + b_L$

complexity.train: $O(E \cdot n \cdot P)$ ($E$ = number of epochs, $P \approx \sum_{l} h_l h_{l+1}$)

pros: Extremely flexible; supports multi-task and multi-output learning
Handles high-cardinality categorical features via embedding layers
Easy to integrate with other deep models
use: Large-sample problems with complex feature interactions
As a component of other architectures
cons: Usually loses to GBDT on small to medium tabular datasets
Requires feature standardization and extensive tuning
Non-convex optimization; results vary with initialization
Poor interpretability
hp: Start with 2–3 layers of 128–512 neurons each
The most important; with Adam, start at 1e-3 and use a learning-rate schedule
Use validation loss to decide when to stop

leaves.name: TabPFN
leaves.plain: A Transformer pre-trained in advance on millions of "fake datasets," so it has already learned how to learn from small data. Given your small tabular dataset, it needs no training: it takes one look and predicts. Well suited to classification and regression with few samples (up to about 10,000 rows).
leaves.intuition: It learns the learning algorithm itself: a Transformer is pre-trained on millions of synthetic datasets generated from random structural causal models, so that, given a training set, it directly outputs the posterior predictive distribution for the test points. At prediction time there are no gradient updates; a single forward pass performs both fitting and prediction (in-context learning), approximating Bayesian inference. Version 2 was published in Nature (2025).
leaves.objective:
Pre-training: $\min_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{D \sim p(D)} \left[ -\log q_\theta(y_{\text{test}} \mid x_{\text{test}}, D_{\text{train}}) \right]$, with $D$ drawn from a synthetic-data prior
Inference: $p(y \mid x, D_{\text{train}}) \approx q_\theta(y \mid x, D_{\text{train}})$

complexity.train: No training phase on the user side; only a single forward pass
complexity.infer: Attention cost grows roughly quadratically with the number of samples; the officially recommended scale is about ≤ 10,000 samples and ≤ 500 features (v2)

pros: Often beats a well-tuned GBDT on small data
Needs almost no tuning; finishes in seconds
use: Fast, strong baseline for small tabular data
Small-sample studies in medicine and science
cons: Caps on the number of samples and features
Needs a GPU to be fast
Black-box model; requires post-hoc explanation methods
Check the license and version-specific terms
hp: Number of internal ensemble members (combinations of different preprocessing and feature permutations); higher is more stable but slower
Beyond the recommended limits, subsample or ensemble over partitions
Designed to need almost no tuning

children.name: 1D Sequential Data
children.def: Elements within a sample are ordered and depend on one another, e.g. text, time series, speech, event logs.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: how sequential dependence is modeled (explicit statistics, hidden-state probabilities, recurrence, convolution, attention)

children.name: Statistical Time-Series Models
children.philosophy: Explicitly captures autocorrelation, trend and seasonality with a small number of interpretable parameters; parameter estimation is backed by a complete statistical theory (confidence intervals, hypothesis tests).

leaves.name: ARIMA / SARIMA
leaves.plain: Predicts the future from the series' own past: today's value depends on the values of the previous few days and on the forecast errors from those days. If the series has a trend, it is first differenced to make it stationary; SARIMA adds seasonality on top (for example, weekly or yearly cycles). A classic, interpretable baseline for time series.
leaves.intuition: Difference the series d times to make it stationary, then forecast the next period as a linear combination of past observations (AR, order p) and past forecast errors (MA, order q). SARIMA adds the corresponding seasonal terms.
leaves.objective:
$\phi(B)(1 - B)^d y_t = \theta(B)\, \varepsilon_t$
$\phi(B) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i B^i$, $\theta(B) = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{q} \theta_j B^j$, $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathrm{WN}(0, \sigma^2)$
Estimated by maximum likelihood; orders selected by AIC / BIC

complexity.train: $O(nr^2)$ per likelihood evaluation (Kalman filter, $r = \max(p, q+1)$) $\times$ number of iterations

cons: Linear and univariate (exogenous variables require ARIMAX)
Requires stationarity tests and manual interpretation of the ACF / PACF
Each series must be modeled separately, which is hard to scale
Long-horizon forecasts converge to the mean
hp: Choose d with ADF / KPSS tests; choose p, q from the ACF / PACF or auto_arima (AIC)
For example, s = 12 for monthly data
Whether to include a constant or drift term

leaves.name: Prophet
leaves.plain: Breaks a time series into three building blocks (long-term trend, weekly/yearly seasonality, and holiday effects), estimates each separately, and adds them up. It is forgiving of missing values and outliers and has intuitive parameters, making it a quick way to forecast business data with clear cycles (traffic, sales).
leaves.intuition: Decomposes a time series into interpretable additive components: y(t) = trend g(t) + seasonality s(t) + holidays h(t) + ε. The trend is piecewise linear (or logistic with saturation) with automatically detected changepoints, and seasonality is represented by a Fourier series. At heart it is curve fitting rather than autoregression, so it tolerates missing values and irregular spacing.
leaves.objective:
$y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + \varepsilon_t$
$s(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \Big[ a_n \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n t}{P}\right)$
$\qquad + b_n \sin\left(\frac{2\pi n t}{P}\right) \Big]$
MAP estimation with Stan; Laplace prior on changepoint magnitudes (encourages sparsity)

complexity.train: $O(n(N + C))$ per iteration, where $N$ is the number of Fourier terms and $C$ the number of changepoints

pros: Business users can understand and manually adjust it
Handles multiple seasonalities and holidays automatically
Robust to missing values and outliers
use: Forecasting daily or weekly business metrics
cons: Ignores autocorrelation structure; residuals are often serially correlated
Several benchmark studies show it often loses to well-tuned ARIMA / ETS or GBDT
Not suited to high-frequency data
hp: The most important; controls trend flexibility, roughly 0.001–0.5
Proportion of the history in which changepoints may occur

children.name: Probabilistic Graphical Sequence Models
children.philosophy: Describes Markov dependence between sequence elements with hidden states or conditional random fields, and performs exact inference by dynamic programming.

leaves.name: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
leaves.plain: Behind the scenes, unseen "states" are switching (for example, whether the market is bullish or bearish, or which sound a person is making), and we only see the surface signals they produce. An HMM works backward from the observed sequence to infer the most likely sequence of hidden states.
leaves.intuition: Behind the observations lies an unseen chain of discrete states: the states evolve according to a transition matrix, and each state generates an observation from its emission distribution. The forward–backward algorithm computes the likelihood, and the Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely state path.
leaves.objective:
$p(x_{1:T}, z_{1:T}) = \pi(z_1) \prod_{t=2}^{T} A(z_{t-1}, z_t)$
$\qquad \times \prod_{t=1}^{T} B(z_t, x_t)$
Maximize $\log p(x)$ with Baum-Welch (EM)
Decoding: $z^* = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{z} p(z \mid x)$ (Viterbi)

complexity.train: $O(TS^2)$ per sequence per EM iteration, where $S$ is the number of states

cons: Overly strong assumptions: first-order Markov states and conditionally independent observations
EM converges only to a local optimum
As a generative model, it struggles to use many overlapping features
hp: Number of states; choose by BIC
Covariance form for a Gaussian HMM
Run multiple random initializations and keep the best
leaves.note: With labeled data, the parameters can be estimated directly from counts (supervised); without labels, use Baum-Welch (unsupervised). It is classified here under its most typical use, sequence labeling.

leaves.name: Conditional Random Field (CRF)
leaves.plain: When labeling a sequence (for example, tagging each word in a sentence as a person name, a place name, or other), it looks not only at each word itself but also at whether neighboring labels make sense together. For example, "middle of a person name" is unlikely to be followed directly by "start of a place name." Judging the whole sentence at once is more consistent than labeling word by word.
leaves.intuition: Models p(y | x) directly (discriminative) and considers the entire label sequence jointly: feature functions describe transitions between labels and the compatibility between labels and observations, and normalization is global over the whole sequence, which avoids the label bias problem of MEMMs.
leaves.objective:
$p(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \exp\Big($
$\quad \sum_{t} \sum_{k} \lambda_k f_k(y_{t-1}, y_t, x, t) \Big)$
Maximize the conditional log-likelihood + $L_2$ regularization; $Z(x)$ is computed with the forward algorithm

complexity.train: $O(T \cdot Y^2 \cdot F)$ per sequence per iteration, where $Y$ is the number of labels and $F$ the number of active features

pros: Can use many arbitrary, overlapping observation features
Global normalization keeps label sequences consistent
Often stacked on top of a BiLSTM or BERT to improve labeling consistency
use: Chinese word segmentation and part-of-speech tagging
cons: Slower to train than an HMM
Requires hand-crafted features when not paired with a neural network
The Y² cost is high when there are many labels
hp: Context window, word shape, capitalization, etc.

children.name: Recurrent Neural Networks
children.philosophy: Compresses the entire history into a recurrent hidden state $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$, shares parameters across time, and trains with backpropagation through time (BPTT).

leaves.name: LSTM
leaves.plain: A neural network with "memory": it reads data in order and uses three gates to decide what to remember, what to forget, and what to output. As a result, it can hold on to information from further back, and it was once widely used for text, speech, and time series.
leaves.intuition: In a vanilla RNN, gradients are multiplied repeatedly across time steps and easily vanish or explode. The LSTM adds a cell state cₜ that is updated additively, with forget, input, and output gates controlling what information is kept and written, so gradients can flow along cₜ over long distances almost without loss (the constant error carousel).
leaves.objective:
$f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f)$, $i_t = \sigma(\cdots)$, $o_t = \sigma(\cdots)$, $\tilde{c}_t = \tanh(\cdots)$
$c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t$
$h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)$
The loss depends on the task (cross-entropy or MSE); optimized with BPTT

complexity.train: $O(T \cdot h \cdot (h + d))$ per sequence (four gates); cannot be parallelized over time

pros: Learns long-range dependencies better than a vanilla RNN
Naturally handles variable-length sequences and streaming data
Far fewer parameters than a Transformer
cons: Computation is sequential over time, so training is slow
Very long dependencies remain difficult
Largely replaced by Transformers in NLP
hp: Can be enabled for non-causal tasks (e.g., labeling)
Use truncated BPTT for very long sequences

leaves.name: GRU
leaves.plain: A streamlined version of the LSTM that cuts the gates from three to two. It has fewer parameters and trains faster, and on most tasks it performs about as well as an LSTM.
leaves.intuition: A streamlined LSTM: the forget and input gates are merged into a single update gate zₜ, and the separate cell state is removed. It has about 25% fewer parameters and performs similarly to an LSTM on most tasks.
leaves.objective:
$z_t = \sigma(W_z [h_{t-1}, x_t])$, $r_t = \sigma(W_r [h_{t-1}, x_t])$
$\tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W [r_t \odot h_{t-1}, x_t])$
$h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t$

complexity.train: $O(T \cdot h \cdot (h + d))$ (three gates, about 3/4 of an LSTM)

pros: Faster than an LSTM, with fewer parameters
Less prone to overfitting on small data
use: Same as LSTM; try it first when resources are limited or the dataset is moderately sized
cons: Subject to the same sequential-computation bottleneck as other RNNs
Sometimes slightly worse than an LSTM on very long sequences

children.name: Convolutional Sequence Models
children.philosophy: Replaces recurrence with 1D causal convolutions: local weight sharing, parallel computation across all time steps, and dilation to enlarge the receptive field.

leaves.name: Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN)
leaves.zh: Causal, dilated convolutional network for sequences
leaves.plain: Processes sequences with convolutions instead of recurrence: each step looks only at the past (no peeking at the future), and dilated convolutions, which look back in skips, let just a few layers reach far into the past. Everything runs in parallel, so training is faster and more stable than with an LSTM.
leaves.intuition: Uses causal convolutions that see only the past, with exponentially growing dilation rates (1, 2, 4, 8, …) so that the receptive field expands exponentially with depth, combined with residual connections. All time steps can be computed in parallel, and gradient paths are short and stable.
leaves.objective:
Dilated convolution: $(F *_d x)(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} f(i) \cdot x_{t - d \cdot i}$
Receptive field $R = 1 + (k - 1) \cdot \sum_{l} d_l$
Residual block: $o = \operatorname{ReLU}(x + \mathcal{F}(x))$

complexity.train: $O(L \cdot T \cdot k \cdot C^2)$ ($C$ = number of channels, $L$ = number of layers); parallelizable
complexity.infer: With caching, $O(L \cdot k \cdot C^2)$ per step

cons: The receptive field has a fixed limit; anything beyond it is invisible
Requires keeping a history buffer at inference time
The network must be redesigned when the dependency length changes
hp: [1, 2, 4, …], so that the receptive field ≥ the required history length

children.name: Self-Attention Architectures
children.philosophy: Drops recurrence and lets every position compute similarity-based weights (attention) directly against every other position, capturing global dependencies in a single step; positional encodings restore order information, and computation is fully parallel.

leaves.name: Transformer (Encoder-Decoder)
leaves.plain: Its core is "attention": when processing each word, it looks at every other word in the sentence to judge which ones are most relevant and how much to draw on each. Because it doesn't have to process words one at a time, computation can be massively parallelized, so it can be trained at very large scale. It is the foundational architecture of modern large language models.
leaves.intuition: Each token produces a Query, Key, and Value; the similarity between Q and K determines how much V to "read" from each position. Multi-head attention learns different relationships in parallel; the encoder understands the input, and the decoder reads the encoded result via cross-attention and generates the output autoregressively. The original paper trained it on supervised machine translation.
leaves.objective:
$\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) V$
$\operatorname{MultiHead} = \operatorname{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, W^O$
Training: minimize the cross-entropy of the target sequence $-\sum_{t} \log p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$ (teacher forcing), often with label smoothing

complexity.train: $O(L^2 d + L d^2)$ per layer; fully parallelizable
complexity.infer: Autoregressive decoding over $L$ steps; with a KV cache, $O(Ld)$ per step
complexity.space: Attention matrix $O(L^2)$ (FlashAttention reduces this to $O(L)$ extra memory)

pros: Scales well with data and model size; the backbone of nearly all foundation models
cons: Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length
Data-hungry; overfits easily on small data
Extrapolating to longer positions requires special designs (RoPE, ALiBi)
hp: Warmup followed by inverse-sqrt or cosine decay; critical
AdamW (β₂ = 0.98); batch size measured in tokens

leaves.name: Temporal Fusion Transformer
leaves.plain: A Transformer built specifically for multi-step time-series forecasting. It can take in static information (store type), known future information (holidays, promotions), and past observations all at once, automatically picks out the important variables, and also provides prediction intervals and interpretable attention weights.
leaves.intuition: An interpretable architecture for multi-horizon forecasting: variable selection networks automatically pick out important features, an LSTM handles local temporal patterns, and multi-head attention captures long-term patterns. It routes static covariates, known future inputs (holidays, promotions), and historical observations through separate paths, and directly outputs quantile forecasts.
leaves.objective:
Quantile loss: $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{q} \sum_{t} \Big[ q\, (y_t - \hat{y}_t^{q})_+$
$\qquad + (1 - q)(\hat{y}_t^{q} - y_t)_+ \Big]$, $q \in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9\}$

complexity.train: Per sample: attention $O(T^2 d)$ + LSTM $O(Td^2)$
complexity.infer: Same as the forward cost in training

pros: Supports multivariate, multi-horizon, and probabilistic forecasting
Makes good use of known future information
use: Medium- to long-term forecasting across many stores and SKUs
cons: Complex architecture; expensive to train
Needs a relatively large amount of data
Does not necessarily beat GBDT or statistical models on small data

children.name: Regular Grid Data
children.def: Elements sit on evenly spaced grid points, with translational structure and spatial proximity, e.g. images (2D), video (2D + time), medical voxels (3D).
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: strength of the spatial inductive bias (local convolution vs. global attention)

children.name: Convolutional Neural Networks
children.philosophy: Local receptive fields plus weight sharing give translation equivariance and drastically cut the number of parameters; stacked layers form hierarchical features, from edges and textures up to objects.

leaves.name: ResNet
leaves.plain: Stack a neural network too deep and it actually learns worse. ResNet adds a "shortcut" every few layers so the signal can skip straight past them, and the network only has to learn how much to correct what it already has. This small change makes it possible to train networks with over a hundred layers.
leaves.intuition: As networks get deeper, training error actually goes up (the degradation problem). A residual block has each layer learn only a correction F(x), with output x + F(x); the identity shortcut lets gradients flow directly to shallow layers, making it possible to train networks with over a hundred layers.
leaves.objective:
$y = \mathcal{F}(x, \{W_i\}) + x$
For classification, trained with cross-entropy $-\sum_{c} y_c \log \operatorname{softmax}(z)_c$

complexity.train: $O\big(\sum_{l} H_l W_l k^2 C_{l-1} C_l\big)$ per image; ResNet-50 is about 4 GFLOPs ($224^2$; varies depending on whether FLOPs or MACs are counted)

pros: Even very deep networks train stably
Mature hardware optimization; still a strong baseline
use: Feature-extraction backbone for all kinds of vision tasks
cons: Local receptive fields require stacking many layers to see global context
Matched by ViT-family models on very large-scale data
Not inherently invariant to rotation and scale
hp: Decide how many layers to freeze

leaves.name: U-Net
leaves.plain: It first compresses the image step by step to understand what is in it, then scales it back up step by step to mark where things are and what each pixel belongs to, using skip connections to pass details from before compression straight to the upscaling side. It excels at pixel-level segmentation, such as finding tumors in medical images.
leaves.intuition: The encoder progressively downsamples to understand "what," and the decoder progressively upsamples to recover "where"; symmetric skip connections pass high-resolution details directly to the decoder, so precise boundaries can be obtained from few annotations. U-Net is also a common backbone for the denoising network in diffusion models.
leaves.objective:
Pixel-wise cross-entropy $-\sum_{\text{pixels}} w(x) \cdot \log p_{\ell(x)}(x)$ (the original paper weights it to emphasize boundaries)
Often combined with Dice loss: $1 - \frac{2 \lvert P \cap G \rvert}{\lvert P \rvert + \lvert G \rvert}$, to handle foreground imbalance

complexity.train: $O(H \cdot W \cdot C^2 \cdot k^2 \cdot \text{depth})$ per image
complexity.space: $O(H \cdot W \cdot C)$ activations (must be kept for the skip connections)

cons: High memory consumption on high-resolution inputs
Limited global context (can be improved by adding attention)
Needs specialized loss functions under extreme class imbalance

leaves.name: YOLO
leaves.plain: It divides the image into a grid, looks at the whole picture in one go, and simultaneously predicts where the objects are, how big their boxes are, and what they are. Because it only looks once (You Only Look Once), it is fast enough for real-time detection, for example in surveillance cameras and self-driving cars.
leaves.intuition: Treats detection as a single-pass regression: the whole image is seen once, each grid cell or feature point simultaneously predicts box coordinates, objectness, and class probabilities, and non-maximum suppression (NMS) then removes duplicate boxes. Its speed allows real-time operation; it has since been iterated through versions such as v8 and YOLO11.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L} = \lambda_{\text{box}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}} + \lambda_{\text{obj}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{obj}} + \lambda_{\text{cls}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}$: CIoU / GIoU; $\mathcal{L}_{\text{obj}}$, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$: BCE
After inference, NMS (IoU threshold) removes duplicate boxes

complexity.train: One forward and one backward pass per image
complexity.infer: A single forward pass, from a few to several hundred GFLOPs depending on model size; real-time on a GPU

pros: Complete deployment ecosystem (ONNX, TensorRT, mobile devices)
cons: Weaker on small and densely overlapping objects (improving with each version)
Requires many bounding-box annotations
NMS parameters affect the results
hp: Confidence and overlap thresholds at inference

children.name: Vision Transformers
children.philosophy: Splits an image into fixed-size patches treated as tokens and models global relationships with self-attention; weakens the inductive bias, trading data volume for expressiveness.

leaves.name: ViT
leaves.plain: It cuts an image into small square patches and feeds them into a Transformer as if they were a sequence of words. Unlike a CNN, it doesn't assume that neighboring pixels are more closely related, so it needs a lot of data to learn well; with enough data, it outperforms CNNs.
leaves.intuition: Splits the image into 16×16 patches, linearly projects each into a vector, adds position embeddings and a [CLS] token, and feeds the result into a standard Transformer encoder; the [CLS] output is then used for classification. It lacks the locality bias of CNNs, so it does worse on small data, but after large-scale pre-training it surpasses CNNs.
leaves.objective:
$z_0 = [x_{\text{cls}};\, x_p^1 E;\, \ldots;\, x_p^N E] + E_{\text{pos}}$, $N = HW / P^2$
Classification cross-entropy computed on $\operatorname{LN}(z_L^0)$

complexity.train: $O(N^2 d + N d^2)$ per layer; for a $224^2$ image with $P = 16$, $N = 196$

pros: Integrates naturally with multimodal models (CLIP, VLMs)
use: Image encoder for CLIP and vision-language models
cons: Requires lots of data or strong pre-training (DeiT mitigates this with distillation and strong augmentation)
Token count grows quadratically at high resolution
hp: Strong data augmentation, stochastic depth, mixup
Warmup + cosine; layer-wise learning-rate decay when fine-tuning

leaves.name: Swin Transformer
leaves.plain: An improved ViT: attention is computed only within small windows, and the next layer shifts the windows so information flows across regions; like a CNN, it also reduces resolution layer by layer. This cuts computation dramatically, making it well suited to tasks that need high resolution, such as detection and segmentation.
leaves.intuition: Computes attention only within non-overlapping local windows, making cost linear in image size; the next layer shifts the windows by half a window so neighboring windows exchange information. Patches are then merged layer by layer into hierarchical feature maps, combining the multi-scale structure of CNNs with the flexibility of Transformers.
leaves.objective:
Alternating W-MSA and SW-MSA (shifted windows)
Complexity: $\Omega(\text{W-MSA}) = 4hwC^2 + 2M^2 hwC$ (linear in $hw$)
Compared with global attention: $\Omega(\text{MSA}) = 4hwC^2 + 2(hw)^2 C$

complexity.train: $O(hw M^2 C + hw C^2)$ per layer
complexity.space: Linear in the number of tokens

pros: Hierarchical features suit dense prediction such as detection and segmentation
State of the art on several benchmarks at publication
cons: More complex to implement (window shifting and masking)
Deployment optimization less mature than for pure CNNs

children.name: Arbitrary Graph-Structured Data
children.def: Elements are connected by irregular edges, with a variable number of neighbors and no ordering, e.g. social networks, molecules, transaction networks, knowledge graphs.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: how far information propagates over the graph (hop-by-hop message passing vs. global attention)

children.name: Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks
children.philosophy: Each node repeatedly "collects messages from its neighbors → aggregates → updates its own representation", so k layers see a k-hop neighborhood; the model is invariant to the ordering of nodes.

leaves.name: GCN
leaves.plain: Learns on "graphs" such as social networks and molecular structures: each node gathers information from its neighbors and averages it to update itself, and after a few stacked layers it can "see" friends of friends. Commonly used for node classification, such as flagging fraudulent accounts.
leaves.intuition: Generalizes image convolution to graphs: a symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix takes a weighted average over neighbors, followed by a linear transformation and an activation. It can be viewed as a first-order approximation of spectral graph convolution.
leaves.objective:
$H^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left( \tilde{D}^{-1/2} \tilde{A} \tilde{D}^{-1/2} H^{(l)} W^{(l)} \right)$, $\tilde{A} = A + I$
The original paper targets semi-supervised node classification: cross-entropy is computed only on labeled nodes

complexity.train: $O(L \cdot (Ed + Vd^2))$
complexity.space: $O(E + Vd)$ (full-batch training requires loading the entire graph)

pros: Simple and effective, with few parameters
use: Node attribute prediction in knowledge graphs
cons: Transductive: new nodes require recomputation
Oversmooths as layers are added: node representations become nearly identical
Full-graph training is memory-intensive

leaves.name: GraphSAGE
leaves.plain: Instead of using every neighbor, it samples just a subset of neighbors each time to pool their information, and learns a general rule for "how to pool." That lets it handle enormous graphs and apply directly to new nodes never seen during training (e.g., newly registered users).
leaves.intuition: Rather than learning a fixed embedding for each node, it learns an "aggregation function": for each node, sample a fixed number of neighbors, aggregate them (mean, LSTM, or pooling), and concatenate the result with the node's own representation. This makes it inductive: it can run inference on new nodes directly, and it scales to large graphs through mini-batch sampling.
leaves.objective:
$h_{\mathcal{N}(v)}^{k} = \operatorname{AGG}\left( \{ h_u^{k-1},\ u \in S(\mathcal{N}(v)) \} \right)$
$h_v^{k} = \sigma\left( W^{k} \cdot \operatorname{CONCAT}(h_v^{k-1},\, h_{\mathcal{N}(v)}^{k}) \right)$, followed by $\ell_2$ normalization
Trained with a supervised cross-entropy loss or an unsupervised neighborhood-proximity loss with negative sampling

complexity.train: $O\big(\prod_{k} S_k \cdot d^2\big)$ per node ($S_k$ = number of neighbors sampled at layer $k$); supports mini-batching

pros: Scales to billions of edges (e.g., PinSage)
cons: Neighbor sampling introduces variance
The number of sampled nodes grows exponentially with the number of layers, which limits depth
The choice of aggregator matters a lot

leaves.name: GAT
leaves.plain: When pooling information from neighbors on a graph, it doesn't treat every neighbor the same; it uses attention to learn automatically which neighbors matter more. It's like how your opinions are swayed more by close friends than by casual acquaintances.
leaves.intuition: A neighbor's importance shouldn't be determined by degree alone: an attention mechanism learns a weight $\alpha_{ij}$ for each edge, and multi-head attention stabilizes training.
leaves.objective:
$e_{ij} = \operatorname{LeakyReLU}\left( a^\top [W h_i \mathbin{\Vert} W h_j] \right)$
$\alpha_{ij} = \operatorname{softmax}_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)}(e_{ij})$
$h_i' = \sigma\left( \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \alpha_{ij} W h_j \right)$ (heads concatenated or averaged)

complexity.train: $O(VFF' + EF')$ per head

use: Relational networks where neighbor importance varies widely
cons: The original attention is "static," which limits expressiveness (fixed by GATv2)
Multiple heads increase memory use
Also suffers from over-smoothing

leaves.name: GIN
leaves.plain: The goal is to maximize a graph neural network's "discriminative power": it pools neighbors by summing rather than averaging, so that graphs with different structures end up with different representations wherever possible. Commonly used to classify whole graphs, such as predicting whether a molecule is toxic.
leaves.intuition: The theoretical question: at most, how many different graphs can a GNN tell apart? The answer is that message-passing GNNs are at most as discriminative as the 1-WL graph isomorphism test. Reaching that bound requires an injective aggregation function, so use sum rather than mean or max, followed by an MLP.
leaves.objective:
$h_v^{(k)} = \operatorname{MLP}^{(k)}\Big( (1 + \epsilon^{(k)}) \cdot h_v^{(k-1)}$
$\qquad + \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} h_u^{(k-1)} \Big)$
Graph-level readout: $\operatorname{CONCAT}_{k}\left( \sum_{v} h_v^{(k)} \right)$

complexity.train: $O(L \cdot (Ed + Vd^2))$

pros: Theoretically the most expressive message-passing GNN
use: Graph classification tasks of all kinds
cons: Still bounded by 1-WL; cannot distinguish certain regular graphs
Sum aggregation gives high-degree nodes very large values, so normalization is needed

children.name: Graph Transformers
children.philosophy: Lets every node attend directly to all nodes and encodes graph structure (distances, degrees, edge features) as attention biases, breaking past the locality of message passing.

leaves.name: Graphormer
leaves.plain: Brings the Transformer to graphs: every node can attend directly to every other node, and the model is also told structural facts such as how far apart two nodes are in the graph and how central each one is. It performs exceptionally well at predicting molecular properties.
leaves.intuition: Teaches a Transformer to read graph structure: the shortest-path distance between each pair of nodes becomes an attention bias (spatial encoding), degree-centrality embeddings are added, and edge features along the path are encoded. Every layer sees the entire graph.
leaves.objective:
$A_{ij} = \frac{(h_i W_Q)(h_j W_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d}} + b_{\phi(v_i, v_j)} + c_{ij}$
$\phi$ is the shortest-path distance; $c_{ij}$ is the averaged encoding of edge features along the path
$h_i^{(0)} = x_i + z^{-}_{\deg^{-}(v_i)} + z^{+}_{\deg^{+}(v_i)}$ (centrality encoding)

complexity.train: $O(V^2 d)$ per layer, plus $O(VE)$ shortest-path preprocessing

pros: Best results on molecular property prediction (OGB-LSC PCQM4M) at the time of publication
use: Graph-level prediction on small-to-medium graphs such as molecules and materials
cons: O(V²) cost rules out direct use on large graphs
Needs large amounts of data for pre-training
hp: Number of layers and hidden dimension
Longer distances are merged into a single bucket

children.name: Unsupervised Learning
children.signal: No external target at all: the objective is the geometric or statistical structure of the data itself (distance, density, variance, co-occurrence), and the output is "a description of this particular dataset".
children.criterion: L2 split criterion: type of output (discrete labels for samples / continuous coordinates for samples / how typical each sample is / relationships between variables)

children.name: Clustering
children.def: Output: each sample → a discrete cluster label (or probabilities of belonging to each cluster). The goal is to group similar samples together.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the mathematical definition of a "cluster" (close to a center / dense and connected / one level of a merge tree / a mixture component / a cut along weak links in a graph)

children.name: Centroid / Partitional
children.philosophy: A cluster is defined as "close to some center point"; the objective is within-cluster dispersion, implicitly assuming clusters are convex and of similar size.

leaves.name: K-Means
leaves.plain: Drop K center points anywhere, assign each observation to its nearest center, then move each center to the average position of its group, and repeat until nothing moves. Simple and fast, it works well for groups of similar size and roughly spherical shape, for example as a first pass at customer segmentation. You have to choose K up front.
leaves.intuition: Alternate two steps: assign each point to its nearest center, then move each center to the mean of its cluster. Neither step can increase the within-cluster squared error, so it is guaranteed to converge (but only to a local optimum). Implicit assumption: clusters are spherical, with equal variance and similar size.
leaves.objective: $\min_{C,\,\mu} \sum_{k} \sum_{x \in C_k} \lVert x - \mu_k \rVert^2$ (within-cluster sum of squares, WCSS / inertia)

complexity.train: $O(I \cdot n \cdot K \cdot d)$

pros: Simple and fast; scales to large data (Mini-Batch K-Means)
Cluster centers serve as prototypes, making them easy to interpret
cons: K must be specified in advance
Only suits convex, spherical clusters of similar size
Sensitive to initialization and outliers
Sensitive to feature scale
hp: Choose with the elbow method, silhouette score, or gap statistic
10 or more runs; keep the best

leaves.name: K-Medoids (PAM)
leaves.plain: Similar to K-Means, but each cluster's representative must be a real observation rather than an average. That makes it less sensitive to extreme values, lets it work with any definition of distance (e.g., text similarity), and makes the representatives themselves easier to interpret.
leaves.intuition: Same spirit as K-Means, but each center must be an actual data point (a medoid), and any distance can be used (Manhattan, Gower, edit distance, DTW). Using real observations as representatives makes it more robust to outliers.
leaves.objective: $\min_{M \subset X,\ \lvert M \rvert = K} \sum_{i} \min_{m \in M} \operatorname{dist}(x_i, m)$

complexity.train: PAM: $O(K \cdot (n - K)^2)$ per iteration; FasterPAM: about $O(n^2)$

pros: Centers are representative observations you can interpret directly
use: Mixed numeric and categorical data (Gower distance)
Situations that call for picking out "representative customers"
cons: Much slower than K-Means (quadratic cost)
Still requires specifying K
hp: Choose the same way as for K-Means
Pick a distance that suits the data type

children.name: Density-Based Clustering
children.philosophy: Clusters are high-density connected regions separated by low-density regions; cluster shape is unrestricted, the number of clusters is determined by the data, and low-density points are treated as noise.

leaves.name: DBSCAN
leaves.zh: Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise
leaves.plain: "Wherever it's crowded, that's a cluster": a point with enough neighbors close by is a core point, connected crowded regions join into one cluster, and isolated points are treated as noise. You don't need to set the number of clusters in advance; it finds clusters of any shape and flags outliers automatically.
leaves.intuition: A point with at least minPts points in its ε-neighborhood is a core point; points that are "density-reachable" from core points are chained into a cluster, and the rest are noise. It finds clusters of arbitrary shape and determines the number of clusters automatically.
leaves.objective:
Core point: $\lvert N_{\epsilon}(p) \rvert \ge \text{minPts}$
Cluster = maximal set of mutually density-connected points (defined through graph connectivity; there is no explicit optimization objective)

complexity.train: About $O(n \log n)$ with a spatial index in low dimensions; $O(n^2)$ worst case
complexity.infer: No native support for predicting new points
complexity.space: $O(n)$; $O(n^2)$ if a distance matrix is used

pros: Determines the number of clusters automatically
cons: A single ε cannot handle clusters with very different densities
Distances break down in high dimensions
ε is hard to tune
hp: Plot the k-distance graph (k = minPts − 1) and take the "knee" of the curve

leaves.name: HDBSCAN
leaves.plain: An evolution of DBSCAN. DBSCAN relies on a single "crowdedness threshold," which struggles when some clusters are dense and others sparse; HDBSCAN tries every threshold and automatically picks the most stable clusters. Less tuning, more stable results.
leaves.intuition: Combines DBSCAN's results across all values of ε into a hierarchical tree, then selects the clusters that are "most stable and persist the longest." Mutual reachability distance smooths the density, so clusters of different densities can be found at the same time, and the user only has to set a minimum cluster size.
leaves.objective:
Mutual reachability distance:
$d_{\text{mreach}}(a, b)$
$\quad = \max\big( \text{core}_k(a),\ \text{core}_k(b),\ d(a, b) \big)$
Build an agglomerative hierarchy on its minimum spanning tree, then select the set of clusters that maximizes stability $\sum S(C)$
$S(C) = \sum_{x \in C} (\lambda_x - \lambda_{\text{birth}})$, $\lambda = 1 / \text{distance}$

complexity.train: About $O(n \log n)$ on average in low dimensions; $O(n^2)$ worst case

pros: Provides per-point cluster membership probabilities and outlier scores
use: Clustering embeddings (often right after UMAP, e.g., in BERTopic)
cons: High-dimensional data needs dimensionality reduction first
Sometimes labels many points as noise, which requires tuning
Results are still sensitive to min_samples
hp: The most important one: how large is the smallest cluster that is meaningful for the business?
Larger is more conservative; more points are treated as noise
Merges clusters that are too close together

children.name: Hierarchical Clustering
children.philosophy: A cluster is one cut level of a merge tree (dendrogram); the number of clusters is not preset, and a multiscale clustering structure is obtained in one pass.

leaves.name: Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (Ward)
leaves.plain: Merges from the bottom up: every point starts as its own group, and at each step the two most similar groups are combined until only one is left, drawing a "family tree" along the way. You can cut the tree at any height to decide how many groups you want, and see clearly how closely related the groups are.
leaves.intuition: Each point starts as its own cluster, and the two "closest" clusters are merged repeatedly until only one remains, producing a dendrogram; cutting it at any height yields the corresponding number of clusters. Ward linkage always merges the pair of clusters whose merger increases within-cluster variance the least.
leaves.objective:
Ward merge cost: $\Delta(A, B) = \frac{\lvert A \rvert \lvert B \rvert}{\lvert A \rvert + \lvert B \rvert} \cdot \lVert \mu_A - \mu_B \rVert^2$
Other linkages: single (minimum distance), complete (maximum distance), average (average distance)

complexity.train: $O(n^2 \log n)$ in general; $O(n^2)$ for Ward with the nearest-neighbor chain algorithm
complexity.infer: Does not support predicting new points

pros: No need to preset the number of clusters
The dendrogram offers a multi-scale view
use: Tiered segmentation of small customer bases
cons: O(n²) memory; impractical once n exceeds a few tens of thousands
Merges are greedy and irreversible
Sensitive to noise (single linkage causes chaining)
hp: Set one of the two to choose where to cut
ward works only with Euclidean distance
Adds spatial or graph adjacency constraints

children.name: Probabilistic Mixture Models
children.philosophy: A cluster is one mixture component of a probability distribution; each sample belongs to each cluster with some probability (soft clustering).

leaves.name: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)
leaves.plain: Assumes the data is a blend of several "bell curves" and finds each one's location, size, and shape. Unlike K-Means, it gives a "soft" clustering: this customer is 70% like group A and 30% like group B, and groups can be elliptical.
leaves.intuition: Assumes the data comes from a mixture of K Gaussians, so each point belongs to each cluster with some probability. The EM algorithm alternates: the E-step computes each point's responsibility γ for each component, and the M-step updates the means, covariances, and weights using the weighted observations. K-Means is its limiting case under equal variances and hard assignments.
leaves.objective:
$\max_{\theta} \sum_{i} \log \sum_{k} \pi_k \cdot \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)$
E-step: $\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j} \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}$

complexity.train: $O(I \cdot n \cdot K \cdot d^2)$ (full covariance), plus $O(K \cdot d^3)$ per iteration for matrix inversion

pros: Doubles as a density estimator and a generative model
cons: Local optima; K must be specified
Full covariance causes a parameter explosion in high dimensions
Covariance matrices can become singular
hp: Multiple initializations; initialized with kmeans by default

children.name: Graph / Spectral Clustering
children.philosophy: The data are first represented as a graph (or already are one); clusters are the subgraphs formed by "cutting the fewest, weakest edges".

leaves.name: Spectral Clustering
leaves.plain: First turns the data into a network of "who is similar to whom," then looks for natural places to cut that network apart. It can separate shapes that K-Means can't, such as concentric circles and crescent moons.
leaves.intuition: Build a similarity graph from the data; clustering then becomes a "normalized cut": sever as few and as weak edges as possible. The continuous relaxation of this discrete problem amounts to finding the K eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian with the smallest eigenvalues; in that eigenvector space, clusters that were tangled together become easy to separate, and K-Means finishes the job.
