leaves.objective:
$\min \operatorname{NCut}(A, B) = \frac{\operatorname{cut}(A, B)}{\operatorname{vol}(A)} + \frac{\operatorname{cut}(A, B)}{\operatorname{vol}(B)}$
Relaxation: take the eigenvectors of $L_{\text{sym}} = I - D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}$ for its smallest $K$ eigenvalues

complexity.train: Graph construction $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ + eigendecomposition $O(n^3)$; Lanczos on sparse graphs reduces this substantially
complexity.infer: No native support for predicting new points

pros: Separates non-convex shapes (concentric circles, crescent moons)
cons: Expensive on large data
How the similarity graph is built (σ, k-nearest neighbors) has a huge effect
Still requires specifying K
hp: The eigengap can guide the choice

leaves.name: Louvain / Leiden
leaves.plain: Finds "communities" in a network: groups with dense connections inside and sparse connections between them. The algorithm keeps moving nodes and merging groups to maximize this "tight-knit within the group" quality. Used for clustering social networks and uncovering fraud rings. Leiden is an improved version that fixes a flaw in Louvain.
leaves.intuition: Maximizes modularity, which measures how many more edges fall within communities than would be expected under random pairing. Louvain repeats "move nodes locally → collapse communities into super-nodes"; Leiden (2019) fixes Louvain's flaw of possibly producing disconnected communities and guarantees that every community is connected.
leaves.objective: $Q = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i,j} \left[ A_{ij} - \gamma \cdot \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right] \cdot \delta(c_i, c_j)$, where $\gamma$ is the resolution parameter

complexity.train: Near-linear in practice, about $O(E)$
complexity.infer: Not applicable (clusters the whole graph directly)

pros: Handles graphs with millions of nodes in seconds
Determines the number of communities automatically
use: Single-cell RNA clustering (Scanpy uses Leiden by default)
cons: Resolution limit of modularity: small communities may get merged
Results are stochastic
Non-graph data requires building a kNN graph first
hp: The most important one; controls community size
The k for the kNN graph when data is not a graph

children.name: Dimensionality Reduction and Manifold Embedding
children.def: Output: each sample → a set of low-dimensional continuous coordinates that preserve, as far as possible, some important structure of the original data.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: which structure to preserve (global linear variance / local neighborhood relations / latent generative factors)

children.name: Linear Projections
children.philosophy: Re-expresses the data in a linear basis, with the basis chosen by different criteria (maximum variance, statistical independence, non-negative parts).

leaves.name: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
leaves.plain: When data has many columns, it finds a few new directions that best capture how the data varies, and projects the data onto them. It's like finding the camera angle that best shows the height differences in a group photo. A handful of principal components can keep most of the information, which is useful for dimensionality reduction, denoising, and visualization.
leaves.intuition: Find a set of orthogonal directions that successively maximize the variance of the projected data; this is equivalent to minimizing the squared reconstruction error. The solution is the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, i.e., the SVD of the centered data matrix.
leaves.objective:
$\max_{W:\, W^\top W = I} \operatorname{tr}(W^\top S W)$, $S = \frac{1}{n} X^\top X$ (centered)
$\Leftrightarrow \min_{W} \lVert X - X W W^\top \rVert_F^2$
Solution: $X = U \Sigma V^\top$, $W = V$ truncated to the first $k$ columns

complexity.train: Full SVD $O(\min(n \cdot d^2,\ n^2 \cdot d))$; randomized SVD $O(n \cdot d \cdot k)$

pros: Invertible, so it can be used for denoising
Decorrelates features and provides interpretable explained-variance ratios
use: Dimensionality reduction and removing collinearity before modeling
cons: Captures only linear structure
Driven by the amount of variance, but high variance does not mean useful for the task
Sensitive to scale and outliers
hp: 90–95% cumulative explained variance, or read the scree plot
Whether to scale each component to unit variance
Required when features are in different units

leaves.name: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
leaves.plain: The "cocktail party problem": several microphones record several people talking over one another, and ICA can pull out each person's voice. It requires the original sources to be independent of each other and not bell-shaped. Commonly used for brain-wave data and signal denoising.
leaves.intuition: The cocktail party problem: what we observe is a linear mixture of several independent signals, and the goal is to separate them. By the central limit theorem, a mixture is closer to Gaussian than the original signals, so finding the projection directions that are "least Gaussian" (maximum negentropy) recovers the independent sources.
leaves.objective:
$x = A s$; find $W \approx A^{-1}$ such that the components of $\hat{s} = W x$ are statistically independent
FastICA: $\max J(y) \propto \big[ \mathbb{E}\{G(y)\} - \mathbb{E}\{G(\nu)\} \big]^2$
$G(u) = \log\cosh(u)$, $\nu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$

complexity.train: Whitening $O(n \cdot d^2)$ + iterations $O(I \cdot n \cdot d \cdot k)$

pros: Components need not be orthogonal, so they are closer to the real underlying causes
use: Artifact removal in EEG and fMRI
cons: Cannot determine the order or scale of the components
At most one source can be Gaussian
Assumes linear, instantaneous mixing

leaves.name: Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
leaves.plain: Breaks data down into "a few basic parts × how much of each is used," with no negative numbers allowed, so parts can only be added, never subtracted. The resulting parts are usually easy to interpret: articles break down into topics, faces into eyes, noses, and mouths.
leaves.intuition: Approximately factorizes a non-negative data matrix into two non-negative matrices, V ≈ WH. Because parts can only be added, not subtracted, the result is a parts-based representation: faces decompose into eyes and noses, documents into topics.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{W \ge 0,\, H \ge 0} \lVert V - WH \rVert_F^2$ (or KL divergence $D(V \parallel WH)$)
Multiplicative update: $H \leftarrow H \odot \frac{W^\top V}{W^\top W H}$

complexity.train: $O(I \cdot n \cdot d \cdot k)$
complexity.infer: Requires solving another non-negative least-squares problem

pros: A natural fit for count and intensity data
cons: Non-convex; the solution is not unique and depends on initialization
Requires choosing k
Data must be non-negative

children.name: Nonlinear Manifold / Neighborhood Preservation
children.philosophy: Assumes the data lie on a low-dimensional curved manifold in a high-dimensional space, and prioritizes preserving local neighborhood relations or geodesic distances along the manifold.

leaves.name: t-SNE
leaves.plain: Squeezes high-dimensional data into a 2D plot, focused on one thing: points that were close together should stay close in the picture. It is great at showing clusters neatly separated, but the distances between clusters and the cluster sizes carry no meaning; it's for looking at, not for measuring.
leaves.intuition: Converts "who neighbors whom" in high dimensions into probabilities, then finds positions in 2D or 3D whose neighbor probability distribution matches as closely as possible. The low-dimensional side uses a heavy-tailed Student-t distribution so that moderately distant points can be pushed farther apart; this solves the crowding problem and is why clusters separate so clearly.
leaves.objective:
$p_{j \mid i} \propto \exp\!\left( -\frac{\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2}{2\sigma_i^2} \right)$ ($\sigma_i$ set by perplexity)
$p_{ij} = \frac{p_{j \mid i} + p_{i \mid j}}{2n}$
$q_{ij} \propto \left( 1 + \lVert y_i - y_j \rVert^2 \right)^{-1}$
$\min \mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q) = \sum p_{ij} \log \frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}$

complexity.train: Exact: $O(n^2)$; Barnes-Hut: $O(n \log n)$; FFT-accelerated (FIt-SNE): about $O(n)$

pros: Excellent visualization of local cluster structure
use: Inspecting representations a model has learned
cons: Distances between clusters and cluster sizes are "meaningless"
Cannot transform new data
Results change substantially with perplexity and the random seed
For visualization only; not suitable as downstream features
hp: 5–50, roughly the effective number of neighbors; larger datasets can use larger values
Use 'pca': more stable and preserves more global structure
Reduce to about 50 dimensions with PCA first

leaves.name: UMAP
leaves.plain: A dimensionality-reduction and visualization tool similar to t-SNE, but faster and better at preserving overall structure (where clusters sit relative to one another). It can also transform new data, and is often used as a dimensionality-reduction preprocessing step.
leaves.intuition: Built on Riemannian geometry and topology: assuming the data is uniformly distributed on a manifold, it adaptively builds a weighted kNN graph (a fuzzy simplicial complex) using each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbor, then optimizes a similar graph in low dimensions. The loss is the cross-entropy between the two fuzzy sets, with both attractive and repulsive terms, so it preserves more global structure than t-SNE and is also faster.
leaves.objective:
High-dimensional edge weights: $w_{ij} = \exp\!\left( -\frac{d(x_i, x_j) - \rho_i}{\sigma_i} \right)$, then symmetrized via fuzzy union
Low-dimensional: $v_{ij} = \left( 1 + a \lVert y_i - y_j \rVert^{2b} \right)^{-1}$
$\min \mathrm{CE} = \sum \Big[ w_{ij} \log \frac{w_{ij}}{v_{ij}}$
$\qquad + (1 - w_{ij}) \log \frac{1 - w_{ij}}{1 - v_{ij}} \Big]$

complexity.train: Approximate nearest neighbors (NN-descent), empirically about $O(n^{1.14})$, + negative-sampling SGD $O(n \cdot \text{epochs})$

pros: Fast; scales to millions of points
Can transform new data and reduce to any number of dimensions for use as features
cons: Distances and densities still cannot be fully trusted
Results depend on hyperparameters
The theoretical assumption of a uniform distribution does not always hold
hp: 5–50: small values emphasize local detail, large values global structure
0.0–0.99: smaller values make clusters tighter; use 0.0 before clustering
2 for visualization; 5–50 when used as features

leaves.name: Isomap
leaves.plain: Data may lie on a rolled-up surface, like a "Swiss roll," where straight-line distances are misleading. Isomap instead uses "the distance you would walk along the surface," then unrolls the surface to recover the data's true shape.
leaves.intuition: The true distance between two points on a manifold is the geodesic distance "walking along the manifold," not the straight-line distance. Isomap approximates geodesic distances with shortest paths on a kNN graph, then uses classical MDS to embed the distance matrix in a low-dimensional space, which unrolls the Swiss roll.
leaves.objective:
$D_G =$ shortest-path distances on the kNN graph
Classical MDS: $B = -\tfrac12 J D_G^{(2)} J$; take the top $k$ eigenvectors $Y = V_k \Lambda_k^{1/2}$

complexity.train: Shortest paths $O(n^2 \log n)$ + eigendecomposition $O(n^3)$ (partial decomposition $O(n^2 \cdot k)$)
complexity.infer: New data can be transformed approximately

use: Smooth manifold data (images with continuously varying pose or lighting)
Recovering the intrinsic coordinates of scientific data
cons: Very sensitive to noise and "short-circuit" edges
Distorts manifolds that have holes
O(n²) memory
hp: Too small disconnects the graph; too large creates short circuits

children.name: Probabilistic Latent Factor Models
children.philosophy: Writes down a probabilistic generative story of "how a few latent factors produce the observed data", then infers each sample's latent factors as its low-dimensional representation.

leaves.name: Factor Analysis
leaves.plain: Many observed variables may be driven by a handful of unseen "latent factors." For example, answers to a dozen or more survey questions may really reflect just two attitudes: "satisfaction" and "loyalty." Factor analysis uncovers these latent factors.
leaves.intuition: Assumes the observed variables are generated linearly by a few unobservable latent factors, plus each variable's own noise (with heterogeneous variances). Unlike PCA, factor analysis models "common variance" and "unique variance" separately, so the factors explain the covariation among the variables.
leaves.objective:
$x = \mu + \Lambda z + \epsilon$, $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_k)$, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Psi)$ ($\Psi$ is diagonal)
$\Rightarrow x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\ \Lambda \Lambda^\top + \Psi)$
Estimate $\Lambda$, $\Psi$ by EM or maximum likelihood; a varimax rotation can improve interpretability

complexity.train: $O(I \cdot n \cdot d \cdot k)$ + $O(d \cdot k^2)$

pros: Standard tool in psychometrics and survey analysis
cons: Requires linearity and normality assumptions
Factor rotation is not unique, so interpretation is somewhat subjective
Number of factors must be chosen
hp: Choose via parallel analysis or a scree plot
Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) falls under structural equation modeling

leaves.name: LDA Topic Model
leaves.plain: Assumes each article is a mix of a few topics, and each topic is a set of words that tend to appear together. The model automatically distills topics from a large collection of articles (e.g., "finance" = stock prices, interest rates, central bank…) and tells you what share of each article goes to each topic.
leaves.intuition: Generative story: each document is a mixture of topics (θ ~ Dirichlet(α)), and each topic is a probability distribution over the vocabulary (φ ~ Dirichlet(β)); to write each word, first draw a topic, then draw a word from that topic. Inverting to the posterior gives each document's topic proportions (a low-dimensional representation) and each topic's key words.
leaves.objective:
$p(w, z, \theta, \phi \mid \alpha, \beta)$
$= \prod_{k} p(\phi_k \mid \beta) \cdot \prod_{d} p(\theta_d \mid \alpha)$
$\quad \cdot \prod_{n} p(z_{dn} \mid \theta_d) \cdot p(w_{dn} \mid \phi_{z_{dn}})$
Approximate the posterior with variational inference (ELBO) or collapsed Gibbs sampling

complexity.train: Gibbs sampling $O(I \cdot N_{\text{token}} \cdot K)$; online variational $O(N_{\text{token}} \cdot K)$ per pass
complexity.infer: A few inference iterations per new document

pros: Documents are represented as topic proportions, convenient for downstream analysis
Extends to dynamic or supervised topic models
use: Topic exploration of support tickets and reviews
cons: Bag-of-words assumption ignores word order
Performs poorly on short texts
K must be specified, and topic quality requires human judgment
Now often outperformed by "embeddings + clustering" (e.g., BERTopic)
hp: Smaller means fewer topics per document
Smaller means each topic uses a more concentrated set of words
Stop words and word-frequency thresholds; huge impact

children.name: Density Estimation and Anomaly Detection
children.def: Output: each sample → a "typicality" score (density or anomaly score), used to find rare, unusual samples.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the operational definition of an "anomaly" (easy to isolate / sparser than its neighbors / outside the support boundary / low probability density)

children.name: Isolation-Based
children.philosophy: Anomalies are "few and different", so under random splits they are isolated very quickly; there is no need to estimate density or distance.

leaves.name: Isolation Forest
leaves.plain: Anomalies are "few and different," so they are easy to isolate. If you slice the data at random, cut after cut, a normal point takes many cuts before it stands alone, while an anomaly is cut off in just a few. Using "how quickly a point gets isolated" as the anomaly score is fast and works well on high-dimensional data.
leaves.intuition: Build many trees with random splits. Anomalies are "few and different," so they are usually isolated in just a few splits; the shorter the average path needed to isolate a point, the more likely it is an anomaly.
leaves.objective:
$s(x, n) = 2^{-\mathbb{E}[h(x)] / c(n)}$
$c(n) = 2H(n - 1) - \frac{2(n - 1)}{n}$ (normalizing constant for the average path length; $H$ is the harmonic number)
$s$ close to 1 indicates an anomaly; well below 0.5 indicates normal

complexity.train: $O(t \cdot \psi \cdot \log \psi)$ ($t$ = number of trees, $\psi$ = subsample size, default 256)

pros: Linear time; works in high dimensions
Subsampling makes it very efficient on large datasets
cons: Axis-parallel splits are biased for certain anomaly shapes (improved by Extended IF)
The contamination setting affects the threshold
Less sensitive to local anomalies within clusters
hp: Expected fraction of anomalies; or set your own threshold on the scores
Fraction of features used by each tree

children.name: Neighborhood / Local Density
children.philosophy: Anomaly is relative: a point is a local outlier if it is much sparser than the region where its neighbors lie.

leaves.name: LOF
leaves.plain: Looks at how "sparse" the area around a point is and compares it with its neighbors: if everyone else lives in a busy neighborhood and this point alone lives somewhere remote, it's an anomaly. Suited to data whose density varies from region to region.
leaves.intuition: Compares a point's local reachability density with the average density of its k neighbors. A ratio well above 1 means the point is much sparser than its neighbors, i.e., a local outlier. It can find anomalies in data with uneven density that global methods cannot see.
leaves.objective:
$\text{reach-dist}_k(A, B)$
$\quad = \max\big( k\text{-distance}(B),\ d(A, B) \big)$
$\mathrm{lrd}(A) = 1 \Big/ \operatorname*{mean}_{B \in N_k(A)} \text{reach-dist}_k(A, B)$
$\mathrm{LOF}(A) = \operatorname*{mean}_{B \in N_k(A)} \frac{\mathrm{lrd}(B)}{\mathrm{lrd}(A)}$; about 1 means normal, well above 1 means outlier

complexity.train: Brute force $O(n^2)$; about $O(n \log n)$ with an index in low dimensions
complexity.infer: Requires novelty=True to predict on new points

pros: Adapts to density that varies across regions
cons: Distances break down in high dimensions
Slow on large datasets
Sensitive to k
hp: 20 is common; should exceed the size of the smallest cluster
Set to True to predict on new data

children.name: Boundary-Based
children.philosophy: Learns a boundary (the support set) that encloses most of the normal data; anything that falls outside it is an anomaly.

leaves.name: One-Class SVM
leaves.plain: Trains on normal data only and draws a boundary that encloses "normal"; anything that later falls outside the boundary is flagged as an anomaly. Suited to cases where you have only normal samples and almost no anomalies to learn from.
leaves.intuition: With only normal data, it finds a hyperplane in kernel feature space that separates the data from the origin with maximum margin, which is equivalent to finding the smallest region enclosing most of the data; points outside the boundary are anomalies. The parameter ν is both an upper bound on the fraction of training errors and a lower bound on the fraction of support vectors.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{w,\, \xi,\, \rho} \tfrac12 \lVert w \rVert^2 + \frac{1}{\nu n} \sum_{i} \xi_i - \rho$
s.t. $w^\top \phi(x_i) \ge \rho - \xi_i$, $\xi_i \ge 0$
Decision function $f(x) = \operatorname{sign}(w^\top \phi(x) - \rho)$
use: Novelty detection with only normal samples
cons: Slow on large datasets
Very sensitive to γ and ν, which are hard to tune without labels
Requires standardization
hp: Roughly an upper bound on the expected fraction of anomalies
Switch to SGDOneClassSVM with a kernel approximation (Nystroem)

children.name: Explicit Density Estimation
children.philosophy: Directly estimates the probability density function p(x); low density = rare = potentially anomalous.

leaves.name: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
leaves.plain: Replace every data point with a small hill and stack them all up: you get a smooth distribution curve, a smoother version of a histogram. Points that land where the density is very low may be outliers.
leaves.intuition: Place a small "kernel" (e.g., a Gaussian bell) on each data point and add them all up to get a smooth density surface. The bandwidth h controls the amount of smoothing: too small gives lots of spikes, too large oversmooths.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{n \cdot h^d} \sum_{i} K\!\left( \frac{x - x_i}{h} \right)$
Bandwidth selection: Silverman's / Scott's rule of thumb, or maximize the cross-validated log-likelihood

complexity.train: $O(1)$ (just stores the data)
complexity.infer: $O(n)$ per query; tree structures can speed this up

pros: Nonparametric; no assumption about the shape of the distribution
use: Anomaly detection with a density threshold
cons: Severe curse of dimensionality (difficult beyond roughly d = 6)
Bandwidth choice is critical
Expensive queries
hp: Most important: use GridSearchCV to maximize log-likelihood

leaves.name: Elliptic Envelope (Robust Covariance)
leaves.plain: Assumes normal data form a roughly elliptical cloud. It first estimates the cloud's center and shape with a method that isn't thrown off by extreme values, then flags points too far from the cloud as anomalies. Suited to data with few features and a roughly bell-shaped distribution.
leaves.intuition: Assumes normal data are approximately multivariate normal and uses the Mahalanobis distance to measure how far each point is from the center. But the ordinary mean and covariance get pulled off by anomalies, so it uses the Minimum Covariance Determinant (MCD) instead: find the h points whose covariance matrix has the smallest determinant and use them to estimate the center and shape, which is robust to contaminated data.
leaves.objective:
MCD: among all subsets of size $h$, find the one that minimizes $\det(\Sigma_H)$
Anomaly score: $d^2(x) = (x - \hat{\mu})^\top \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} (x - \hat{\mu})$, which follows a $\chi^2_d$ distribution under normality

complexity.train: FAST-MCD: about $O(I \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ + $O(d^3)$

use: Low- to medium-dimensional, approximately normal operational metrics
cons: Assumes normality and a single mode
Not applicable in high dimensions (d > n/2)
Cannot handle nonlinear structure
hp: Can instead be set from χ² quantiles

children.name: Variable Relationship Mining
children.def: Output: structure "among variables or items" (co-occurrence rules, conditional dependence networks, causal graphs), rather than anything about individual samples.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the form of the relationship (co-occurrence rules among discrete items / conditional independence structure among continuous variables)

children.name: Frequent Itemsets and Association Rules
children.philosophy: In transactional data, finds combinations of items that frequently occur together, then derives "if A then B" rules.

leaves.name: Apriori
leaves.plain: Finds combinations of products that are "often bought together," such as "people who buy diapers often buy beer too." The clever part: if a combination is rare, any larger combination containing it must be rare too, so it can be skipped outright, saving a great deal of computation.
leaves.intuition: Anti-monotonicity: if an itemset is infrequent, none of its supersets can be frequent. So candidates are generated and pruned level by level (1-itemsets, 2-itemsets, …), and rules of the form "if A is bought, then B is bought" are finally derived from the frequent itemsets.
leaves.objective:
$\text{support}(A) = P(A)$
$\text{confidence}(A \to B) = P(B \mid A)$
$\text{lift}(A \to B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A) \cdot P(B)}$
Find itemsets with $\text{support} \ge \text{minsup}$ and rules with $\text{confidence} \ge \text{minconf}$

complexity.train: Exponential in the worst case, $O(2^{\lvert I \rvert})$; in practice about $O\big(\sum_{k} \lvert C_k \rvert \cdot n\big)$, with one database scan per level

pros: Rules are directly interpretable and actionable
cons: Requires multiple database scans; the number of candidates can explode
Very slow with a low support threshold
Generates many rules that must be further filtered by lift and business relevance
hp: Determines the amount of computation and number of rules
Only values above 1 indicate positive association

leaves.name: FP-Growth
leaves.plain: Does the same job as Apriori (finding combinations that often occur together), but first compresses all transactions into a tree with shared prefixes, so it doesn't have to scan the database over and over. Much faster on large datasets.
leaves.intuition: No candidate generation: scan the database only twice, compress the transactions into a prefix-sharing FP-tree, then recursively build a conditional FP-tree for each item to grow the frequent itemsets directly. Typically an order of magnitude faster than Apriori.
leaves.objective:
support, confidence, and lift are defined as in Apriori
Each transaction is inserted into the FP-tree with its items in descending order of frequency

complexity.train: Two database scans + tree mining (depends on data sparsity; still exponential in the worst case)
complexity.space: $O(\text{FP-tree size})$; can be large for dense data

pros: Distributed implementation available in Spark MLlib
cons: The FP-tree may not fit in memory
More complex to implement
Same rule-explosion problem as Apriori
hp: Number of partitions for distributed Spark

children.name: Probabilistic Graph Structure Learning
children.philosophy: Infers the conditional independence structure among variables from data, yielding a dependence network (undirected) or a causal graph (directed).

leaves.name: Graphical Lasso
leaves.plain: For when you want to know "who directly affects whom" among many variables, not just which ones move together. It estimates a sparse network of relationships, keeping only the links that remain correlated after accounting for all other variables and pruning indirect ones, so the network is clear and readable.
leaves.intuition: In a Gaussian model, a zero entry in the precision matrix Θ = Σ⁻¹ means the two variables are conditionally independent given all the others. Adding an L1 penalty on Θ yields a sparse estimate from which the conditional dependence network among variables can be read off directly, distinguishing direct from indirect associations.
leaves.objective: $\max_{\Theta \succ 0} \log\det \Theta - \operatorname{tr}(S\Theta) - \lambda \lVert \Theta \rVert_1$ ($S$ is the sample covariance matrix)

complexity.train: Block coordinate descent, $O(d^3)$ per iteration
complexity.infer: N/A (the output is a network structure)

cons: Requires a Gaussian assumption
Gives only undirected relationships, not causation
The choice of λ determines how sparse the network is
hp: Use GraphicalLassoCV or StARS stability selection

leaves.name: PC Algorithm
leaves.plain: Infers a graph of causal directions from observational data. It first runs a series of tests of the form "after controlling for certain variables, are A and B still correlated?" to prune edges with no direct relationship, then uses specific structures to infer the direction of the arrows. The result still relies on strong assumptions (e.g., no omitted common causes) and should be treated as a hypothesis to be validated.
leaves.intuition: Start from the complete graph and run conditional independence tests on each pair of variables: if they are independent given any conditioning set, delete the edge. Then use v-structures (X → Z ← Y) and orientation propagation rules to orient some of the edges, yielding the Markov equivalence class of the causal graph (a CPDAG).
leaves.objective:
If there exists $S \subseteq \operatorname{adj}(X) \setminus \{Y\}$ with $\lvert S \rvert = \ell$ such that $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid S$ (test $p > \alpha$), delete the edge $X$ – $Y$; increase $\ell$ step by step
Finally, orient the v-structures and apply Meek's rules

complexity.train: Exponential in the maximum degree in the worst case; about $O(d^{k+2})$ tests for sparse graphs ($k$ = maximum number of neighbors)
complexity.infer: N/A (the output is a causal graph)

pros: When its assumptions hold, can infer causal directions from observational data
Nonparametric independence tests can be used
Results can be checked against domain knowledge
use: Building a DAG before causal inference
Exploring dependencies among process and system variables
cons: Relies on causal sufficiency (no hidden confounders) and faithfulness assumptions
A single test error can cascade
Recovers only an equivalence class; some edges cannot be oriented
hp: Fisher-z for continuous, χ² for categorical, KCI for nonlinear
Can add constraints such as temporal ordering

children.name: Self-Supervised and Generative Learning
children.signal: No external labels; instead, a proxy objective is "constructed" from the data itself (a masked-out part, the next token, another augmented view, added noise) to train a parametric model, producing reusable representations or generators.
children.criterion: L2 split criterion: how the proxy objective is constructed (predict missing parts in data space / align different views in representation space / learn a transformation from a prior to the data distribution)

children.name: Predictive (Masked / Autoregressive / Reconstruction)
children.def: Predicts the rest from a partial observation, with the loss computed in "data space" (the next token, masked patches, the original input). There is no generative mapping that starts from noise or a prior.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: which part is predicted (the future / missing or neighboring parts / everything, reconstructed through a bottleneck)

children.name: Autoregressive Modeling (Predicting the Future)
children.philosophy: Uses the chain rule of probability to factor the joint distribution into a sequence of conditionals $p(x) = \prod_t p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$, predicting the next element step by step.

leaves.name: GPT (Decoder-only Transformer)
leaves.plain: It reads an enormous amount of text and practices just one thing: looking at the words so far and guessing the next one. Taken to the extreme, this teaches it grammar, knowledge, and even some degree of reasoning. This kind of model is at the core of chatbots like ChatGPT.
leaves.intuition: Turns the chain rule of probability, $p(x) = \prod_t p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$, directly into the training task: a causal mask lets each position see only the preceding context as it predicts the next token. Every piece of text on the web is a free label; as models scale up, in-context learning and reasoning abilities emerge.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{\theta} \; -\sum_{t} \log p_{\theta}(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ (next-token cross-entropy)
Perplexity $\mathrm{PPL} = \exp(\text{mean negative log-likelihood})$

complexity.train: About $6ND$ FLOPs in total ($N$ = number of parameters, $D$ = number of training tokens); attention is $O(L^2 d)$ per layer
complexity.infer: About $O(N)$ per token + KV cache reads of $O(L d \cdot \text{layers})$

pros: Gets predictably stronger with scale (scaling laws)
Prompts serve as a general-purpose interface
use: Language core of vision-language and multimodal models
cons: Hallucination
Extremely high training and inference costs
Quadratic cost for long contexts
Needs subsequent alignment (SFT, RLHF, DPO) to be truly useful
hp: Chinchilla rule: about 20 training tokens per parameter

leaves.name: Mamba
leaves.plain: When a Transformer reads long text, every word has to be compared with every other word, so the longer the text, the slower it gets. Mamba works more like a person: it updates a running "summary memory" as it reads and decides from the content what to remember or ignore, so it is much faster and uses far less memory on very long sequences.
leaves.intuition: State space models compress history with a linear recurrence, so cost grows linearly with length; but classic SSMs have fixed parameters and cannot "decide what to remember based on content." Mamba makes B, C, and Δ vary with the input (selectivity) and implements this with a hardware-aware parallel scan, approaching Transformer quality on language modeling in linear time.
leaves.objective:
Continuous form: $h'(t) = A h(t) + B x(t)$, $y(t) = C h(t)$
Discretization: $\bar{A} = \exp(\Delta A)$, $\bar{B} \approx \Delta B$; $h_t = \bar{A} h_{t-1} + \bar{B} x_t$, $y_t = C h_t$
Selectivity: $B,\ C,\ \Delta = f(x_t)$
Training objective is the same as GPT's: next-token cross-entropy

complexity.train: $O(L d N)$, where $N$ is the state dimension; linear in sequence length
complexity.infer: $O(1)$ per token: fixed-size state, no KV cache needed

pros: Constant inference memory and high throughput
use: Very long sequences (genomics, audio, long documents)
Hybrid architectures interleaved with attention layers (e.g., Jamba)
cons: The fixed-size state makes exact recall and copying (long-range retrieval) weaker than with attention
Ecosystem and tooling less mature than for Transformers
hp: Configuration when interleaving with attention layers
leaves.note: Mamba is an architecture; here it is classified by the "autoregressive language modeling" objective demonstrated in its original paper.

children.name: Masked and Context Prediction (Predicting Missing or Neighboring Parts)
children.philosophy: Randomly masks part of the input, or picks out one element, and asks the model to predict the masked part or the co-occurring neighbors from the remaining context.

leaves.name: BERT
leaves.plain: It practices "fill in the blank": some words in a sentence are hidden, and the model guesses them by looking at the text on both sides at once. Because it sees the full context, it has a strong grasp of meaning and suits "understanding" tasks such as classification, search, and question answering, rather than writing articles.
leaves.intuition: Randomly mask 15% of the tokens and have the encoder recover them using the text on both sides at once (MLM), thereby learning bidirectional understanding. The resulting contextualized representations can then be fine-tuned with just a small classification head for classification, NER, and question answering.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MLM}} = -\sum_{i \in M} \log p(x_i \mid x_{\setminus M})$ ($M$ = masked positions)
Masking strategy: 80% replaced with [MASK], 10% with a random token, 10% left unchanged
The original also used NSP (next sentence prediction), which RoBERTa later showed can be removed

complexity.train: $O(L^2 d + L d^2)$ per layer
complexity.infer: A single forward pass; no autoregressive loop

pros: Bidirectional context; strong on understanding tasks
Fast inference with a single forward pass
cons: Cannot directly generate long text
[MASK] appears only in pre-training, causing a pre-training/fine-tuning mismatch
Maximum length of 512 in the original

leaves.name: MAE
leaves.plain: Fill-in-the-blank for images: hide most of a picture (about 75%) and have the model reconstruct the whole image from the remaining fragments. To do that, it has to learn what objects look like, and the features it learns can be reused for all kinds of vision tasks.
leaves.intuition: Images are highly redundant, so the task is only challenging when most of the image is masked: randomly mask 75% of the patches, have the encoder process only the visible 25% (cutting compute by more than 3×), then have a lightweight decoder reconstruct the masked pixels. The learned encoder is a powerful visual representation.
leaves.objective: $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|M|} \sum_{i \in M} \lVert x_i - \hat{x}_i \rVert^2$ (MSE computed only on masked patches; the targets are normalized pixels)

complexity.train: The encoder processes only 25% of patches, about $O((0.25N)^2 d)$; the decoder is lightweight
complexity.infer: Standard ViT forward pass when used downstream

use: Domains with lots of unlabeled images, such as medical imaging and remote sensing
cons: Linear-probe performance trails contrastive methods; usually needs fine-tuning
Pixel reconstruction is biased toward low-level details

leaves.name: Word2Vec
leaves.plain: "You can tell a word by the company it keeps." Based on each word's context, it turns every word into a vector of numbers; words with similar meanings get similar vectors, and it can even do "king − man + woman ≈ queen."
leaves.intuition: Distributional hypothesis: a word's meaning is determined by its neighbors. Skip-gram predicts the surrounding words from the center word (CBOW does the reverse) and uses negative sampling to turn the expensive softmax into binary classification. The learned vectors have a linear analogy structure: king − man + woman ≈ queen.
leaves.objective:
Skip-gram + negative sampling:
$\max \; \log \sigma\big(v'^{\top}_{w_O} v_{w_I}\big)$
$+ \sum_{k} \mathbb{E}_{w_k \sim P_n(w)} \big[ \log \sigma\big(-v'^{\top}_{w_k} v_{w_I}\big) \big]$
$P_n(w) \propto U(w)^{3/4}$

complexity.train: $O(T c K d)$ per epoch ($T$ = number of corpus tokens, $c$ = window size, $K$ = number of negative samples)

pros: Extremely fast; scales to billion-word corpora
Vectors have an interpretable analogy structure
use: Recommender systems (item2vec: treat item sequences as sentences)
cons: Static vectors cannot handle polysemy
Out-of-vocabulary problem (FastText solves it with subwords)
Largely superseded by contextual embeddings
hp: 1 for skip-gram (better for rare words), 0 for CBOW
Word-frequency threshold and number of training epochs

leaves.name: Node2Vec
leaves.plain: Word2Vec, brought to networks: take random walks across the graph, treat each sequence of visited nodes as a sentence, and learn a vector for every node. Nodes with a similar structure or position end up with similar vectors, which is useful for recommendations and link prediction.
leaves.intuition: Turn the graph into "sentences": run biased random walks to generate node sequences, then learn node vectors with Skip-gram. The parameters p and q steer the walk toward BFS (capturing structural roles) or toward DFS (capturing community homophily).
leaves.objective:
$\max \sum_{u \in V} \log P\big(N_S(u) \mid f(u)\big)$, where $N_S(u)$ is the neighborhood obtained from the random walks
Transition bias: $\alpha_{pq}(t, x) = \frac{1}{p}$ (return to the previous node), $1$ (distance 1), $\frac{1}{q}$ (move away)

complexity.train: Walks: $O(V r l)$ ($r$ = walks per node, $l$ = walk length) + Skip-gram training
complexity.space: $O(V d + E)$; precomputing second-order transition probabilities can take more

pros: Embeddings plug directly into downstream models
cons: Transductive: new nodes require retraining
Ignores the nodes' own attribute features
Largely surpassed by GNNs
hp: q < 1 favors DFS, q > 1 favors BFS

children.name: Reconstructive Autoencoding (Reconstructing Everything Through a Bottleneck)
children.philosophy: Forces the data through a narrow bottleneck (or adds noise) and then reconstructs them, so the network can retain only the most important structure.

leaves.name: Autoencoder / Denoising Autoencoder
leaves.plain: Compress the data into a tiny summary, then try to rebuild the original from it. To rebuild it well, that summary has to capture the most important features. The denoising version deliberately adds noise first, so the model learns to recover the clean version. Samples it rebuilds badly (a large reconstruction error) are often flagged as anomalies.
leaves.intuition: Force the data through a narrow bottleneck and then reconstruct it, so the network has no choice but to learn the most important compressed representation. The denoising variant corrupts the input with noise and asks for the clean version back, forcing the model to learn the structure of the data manifold rather than the identity mapping. Under squared error, the optimal subspace of a linear autoencoder is exactly the PCA subspace.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{\theta, \phi} \sum_i \lVert x_i - g_{\phi}(f_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_i)) \rVert^2$
$\tilde{x} = x + \text{noise}$ (DAE) or $\tilde{x} = x$ (standard AE); sparsity or contractive regularization can be added

complexity.train: $O(E n P)$

use: Anomaly detection (high reconstruction error flagged as anomalous)
cons: Unstructured latent space, so you cannot sample from it directly to generate (the problem VAEs solve)
Can learn the identity mapping when there is no bottleneck or noise
Reconstruction error is not the same as semantic similarity
hp: Set from a quantile of the reconstruction error

children.name: Joint-Embedding (Aligning Different Views)
children.def: Different views of the same sample (two data augmentations, an image and its text, visible and masked blocks) should agree in "representation space"; the loss is computed in representation space, without reconstructing the raw data.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: how to avoid representation collapse (the trivial solution in which every input maps to the same point): negative-sample repulsion / asymmetric self-distillation / information regularization

children.name: Contrastive (Negative-Sample Repulsion)
children.philosophy: Pulls positive pairs together and pushes negatives apart; the repulsion from negative samples naturally prevents all representations from collapsing to a single point.

leaves.name: SimCLR
leaves.zh: A simple framework for contrastive learning
leaves.plain: Take one image and alter it in two different ways (cropping, color changes), then tell the model: "these two are the same thing, so pull them together, and push them away from every other image." Without any labels, it learns excellent image features.
leaves.intuition: Two random augmentations of the same image form a "positive pair"; every other image in the batch is a negative. Training pulls positive pairs together in representation space and pushes negative pairs apart. The choice of augmentations defines which variations (color, cropping) the model should "not care about".
leaves.objective:
NT-Xent: $\ell_{i,j} = -\log \frac{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(z_i, z_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k \neq i} \exp(\operatorname{sim}(z_i, z_k)/\tau)}$
$\operatorname{sim}$ is cosine similarity; $z = g(f(x))$ passes through the projection head

complexity.train: Per-batch similarity matrix $O(B^2 d)$ + encoder cost
complexity.space: Requires large batches (4096 in the original paper)

cons: Needs very large batches (many negatives)
Highly sensitive to the combination of augmentations
False negatives: images of the same class are treated as negatives
hp: Random crop + color jitter matter most
MLP; downstream tasks use the representation before the projection head

leaves.name: CLIP
leaves.plain: Trained on hundreds of millions of "image + caption" pairs from the web, it places matching images and text close together in one shared space. Once trained, you can search images with text directly, or classify without any further training (zero-shot), for example by asking "Does this look more like 'a dog' or 'a cat'?"
leaves.intuition: Treat roughly 400 million web "image + caption" pairs as naturally occurring matches: an image encoder and a text encoder pull matching image-text pairs together and push non-matching ones apart. The result is a shared image-text embedding space where text descriptions can be used directly for zero-shot classification and retrieval.
leaves.objective:
Symmetric InfoNCE: $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2} \big[ \mathrm{CE}(S, I) + \mathrm{CE}(S^\top, I) \big]$
$S_{ij} = \tau^{-1} \cdot \langle f_{\text{img}}(x_i), f_{\text{txt}}(t_j) \rangle$ (embeddings are L2-normalized); $\tau$ is a learnable temperature

complexity.train: $O(B^2 d)$ logits per batch ($B = 32{,}768$ in the original paper) + two encoders
complexity.infer: Embed once; retrieval is $O(N d)$ or uses approximate nearest neighbors

pros: A key component of text-to-image and vision-language models
use: Text conditioning for diffusion models, or the vision encoder of a VLM
cons: Weak at fine-grained recognition, counting and spatial relations
Inherits biases from web data
Requires massive amounts of paired data and compute
hp: Size of the image and text encoders
Prompt templates (e.g. 'a photo of a {label}') and prompt ensembling
leaves.note: The paired text is a signal that occurs naturally on the web rather than being manually annotated for a specific task, so it is classified as self-supervised; the literature also calls this "natural language supervision" or weak supervision.

children.name: Self-Distillation (Asymmetric Architecture)
children.philosophy: Uses no negative samples; relies instead on the asymmetric structure of "online network + momentum (EMA) target network + stop-gradient" to make the trivial solution unstable.

leaves.name: BYOL
leaves.plain: Like SimCLR, it makes two altered versions of the same image have similar representations, but it needs no "negative examples" at all. A slowly updated "teacher network" provides targets for a "student network" to learn from, cleverly keeping the model from taking the lazy route of producing the same output for every image.
leaves.intuition: Avoids collapse without negatives: the online network gets an extra prediction head that predicts the target network's representation of the other augmented view; the target network is an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network's weights and receives no gradients. This asymmetry, combined with the stop-gradient, makes the trivial "output a constant for everything" solution unstable.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L} = \left\lVert \frac{q_{\theta}(z_{\theta})}{\lVert q_{\theta}(z_{\theta}) \rVert} - \frac{z'_{\xi}}{\lVert z'_{\xi} \rVert} \right\rVert_2^2$ (symmetrized by summing over both views)
Target network update: $\xi \leftarrow \tau \xi + (1 - \tau) \theta$

complexity.train: Two forward passes per pair (online + target); no $B^2$ negative-pair computation needed

pros: No need for negatives or very large batches
Less sensitive to the choice of augmentations
use: Self-supervised learning when batch size is limited
cons: Why it avoids collapse is not yet fully understood theoretically
Sensitive to the EMA coefficient and the prediction-head design
hp: Raised from 0.996 to 1 on a cosine schedule

leaves.name: DINOv2
leaves.plain: A student network learns to mimic a teacher network's view of different crops of the same image (self-distillation), trained on a large collection of curated images without any labels. The visual features it learns are extremely general and perform strongly out of the box for classification, segmentation and depth estimation.
leaves.intuition: Self-distillation: the student sees local crops, the teacher (an EMA of the student) sees global crops, and the student aligns its output distribution with the teacher's; the teacher's outputs are centered and sharpened to prevent collapse. DINOv2 adds iBOT's patch-level masking objective and trains on 142 million curated images, producing general-purpose visual features that can be used frozen.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L} = -\sum P_t(x) \cdot \log P_s(x')$
$P_t = \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{g_t(x) - c}{\tau_t}\right)$, $P_s = \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{g_s(x')}{\tau_s}\right)$, $\tau_t < \tau_s$ (sharpening), $c$ is the centering vector (EMA)
Teacher update: $\theta_t \leftarrow \lambda \theta_t + (1 - \lambda) \theta_s$

complexity.train: Multi-crop forward passes (2 global + several local) × ViT cost $O(N^2 d)$

pros: Frozen features work for classification, segmentation and depth estimation without fine-tuning
use: Segmentation and depth estimation with few labels
Vision backbone for vision-language models and robotics
cons: Extremely expensive pretraining that requires carefully curated data
Hard to reproduce at small scale
hp: Teacher temperature warmup, number of multi-crop views

leaves.name: I-JEPA
leaves.plain: Show the model part of an image and ask it to predict the "abstract features" of the hidden regions rather than their pixels. Since it does not have to worry about details like the texture of leaves, the model is pushed toward higher-level semantic understanding, and it is also more efficient than reconstructing pixels.
leaves.intuition: Predict representations, not pixels: from the visible context block, predict the representations of the masked target blocks in representation space (the targets come from an EMA encoder). Not reconstructing pixels means no capacity is wasted on unpredictable details, and there is no reliance on hand-crafted data augmentations.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i} \sum_{j \in B_i} \lVert \hat{s}_{y_j} - s_{y_j} \rVert_2^2$
$\hat{s} = g_{\phi}\big(f_{\theta}(x_{\text{context}}), \text{mask tokens}\big)$, $s = f_{\bar{\theta}}(y)$ (EMA target encoder, stop-gradient)

complexity.train: The ViT encoder processes only the context block, plus the predictor; uses less compute than pixel-reconstruction and multi-view contrastive methods
complexity.space: About the same as a ViT

use: World-model research (V-JEPA extends it to video)
cons: Strongly affected by the masking strategy (block size and ratio)
Smaller ecosystem and fewer application examples

children.name: Information Regularization
children.philosophy: Prescribes the desired statistical properties of the representation directly in the loss (every dimension must have variance, different dimensions must be decorrelated), so the regularization term itself prevents collapse.

leaves.name: VICReg
leaves.plain: A "rule-based" approach to self-supervised learning that asks for three things at once: two versions of the same image should be similar, every feature dimension should vary enough (so they don't all collapse to the same value), and different dimensions shouldn't duplicate each other. It is conceptually clear and needs no negative examples.
leaves.intuition: Three regularization terms spell out directly what a good representation looks like: invariance (the embeddings of the two views should be close), variance (the batch standard deviation of each dimension must not get too small, which prevents collapse) and covariance (different dimensions should be decorrelated, which prevents redundant information). No negatives, momentum encoder or stop-gradient required.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L} = \lambda\, s(Z, Z') + \mu \big[ v(Z) + v(Z') \big]$
$\qquad + \nu \big[ c(Z) + c(Z') \big]$
$s = \mathrm{MSE}$; $v(Z) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_j \max\big(0, \gamma - \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(z_j) + \epsilon}\big)$; $c(Z) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i \neq j} [C(Z)]_{ij}^2$

complexity.train: Per-batch covariance $O(B d^2)$ + encoder

pros: The two branches can differ (suited to multimodal settings)
cons: The three weights need to be balanced
The projection head needs a very large dimension (about 8192) to work well

leaves.name: Barlow Twins
leaves.plain: Make the features of two versions of the same image agree closely dimension by dimension, while different dimensions stay uncorrelated: each dimension does its own job and doesn't store duplicate information. A simple, effective self-supervised method.
leaves.intuition: Inspired by the "redundancy reduction" principle from neuroscience: push the cross-correlation matrix between the embeddings of two augmented views toward the identity matrix. Diagonal entries equal to 1 mean each feature is invariant across the two views; off-diagonal entries equal to 0 mean different features are independent of each other and not redundant.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{BT}} = \sum_i (1 - C_{ii})^2 + \lambda \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} C_{ij}^2$
$C_{ij} = \frac{\sum_b z^A_{b,i} z^B_{b,j}}{\sqrt{\sum_b (z^A_{b,i})^2} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_b (z^B_{b,j})^2}}$

complexity.train: Cross-correlation $O(B d^2)$ + encoder

pros: No need for large batches, negatives or an asymmetric architecture
cons: Sensitive to the projection dimension (needs to be high)
λ needs tuning

children.name: Generative (Transforming a Prior into the Data Distribution)
children.def: Learns a mapping from a simple prior (Gaussian noise or latent variables) to the data distribution in order to sample new data; the objective acts on "the entire distribution".
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: how the prior is transformed into the data distribution (variational inference / adversarial game / iterative denoising / invertible mapping or velocity field / energy function)

children.name: Variational Latent Variable Models
children.philosophy: Performs variational inference with an approximate posterior q(z|x), maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO); because the latent space is constrained by the prior, it can be sampled from.

leaves.name: VAE
leaves.plain: Like an autoencoder, it compresses and then reconstructs, but the compressed summary is required to live in a smooth, well-organized space. That means you can pick any point in this space to generate brand-new, plausible samples, or morph smoothly from one face to another.
leaves.intuition: A probabilistic autoencoder: the encoder outputs a distribution over the latent variable, q(z|x), rather than a single point, and the decoder models p(x|z). The ELBO being maximized equals "reconstruction quality − KL divergence from the prior N(0, I)"; the KL term makes the latent space continuous and smooth, so new data can be generated by sampling from the prior. The reparameterization trick z = μ + σ ⊙ ε makes the sampling step differentiable.
leaves.objective:
$\log p(x) \ge \mathrm{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)} \big[ \log p_{\theta}(x \mid z) \big]$
$- \mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \,\Vert\, p(z)\big)$
Reparameterization: $z = \mu_{\phi}(x) + \sigma_{\phi}(x) \odot \epsilon$, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$

complexity.train: $O(E n P)$
complexity.infer: Sampling needs only one decoder forward pass

pros: Smooth latent space that supports interpolation
use: Image compressor for latent diffusion models (the VAE in Stable Diffusion)
cons: Generated samples tend to be blurry
Posterior collapse: a powerful decoder may ignore z
The ELBO is only a lower bound
hp: Values above 1 give more disentangled representations but worse reconstructions
Gradually increase the KL weight to mitigate posterior collapse

leaves.name: VQ-VAE
leaves.plain: Replace the compressed summary with discrete codes from a "codebook", like translating an image into a string of "words" from a limited vocabulary. This lets language models process and generate images or sound just as they do text.
leaves.intuition: Make the latent variable discrete: each encoder output vector is replaced by the nearest codeword in a codebook, so an image becomes a sequence of discrete tokens. First learn the compression, then model the prior over the tokens with an autoregressive model or a Transformer. This is the basic recipe for "tokenizing" images and audio so that language models can handle them.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L} = -\log p(x \mid z_q(x)) + \lVert \operatorname{sg}[z_e(x)] - e \rVert_2^2$
$+ \beta \lVert z_e(x) - \operatorname{sg}[e] \rVert_2^2$
$z_q = e_k$, $k = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_j \lVert z_e(x) - e_j \rVert$ ($\operatorname{sg}$ is the stop-gradient; gradients are passed through with the straight-through estimator)

complexity.train: $O(E n P)$ + an $O(K d)$ nearest-codeword search per latent position

pros: Discrete representations plug easily into Transformers
use: Image and audio tokenizers (VQGAN; the residual quantization in SoundStream / EnCodec follows the same idea)
Input and output tokenization for multimodal language models
cons: Codebook collapse: only a few codewords get used
Needs a second-stage prior model to generate
Straight-through gradients are biased

children.name: Adversarial Generation
children.philosophy: Uses a discriminator as a "learnable distance function"; the generator and discriminator play a zero-sum game until the generated distribution cannot be distinguished from the real one.

leaves.name: GAN
leaves.plain: Two networks face off: a generator tries to produce fakes and a discriminator tries to catch them. Each pushes the other to improve, until the generator creates images that pass for real. Output quality is high, but training is unstable, and sometimes it only produces a handful of variations (mode collapse).
leaves.intuition: A zero-sum game between two networks: the generator turns noise into fake samples and the discriminator tells real from fake, which makes the discriminator a "learnable loss function". At equilibrium the generated distribution equals the data distribution; given the optimal discriminator, the generator is equivalent to minimizing the JS divergence.
leaves.objective:
$\min_G \max_D \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big]$
$+ \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}\big[\log(1 - D(G(z)))\big]$
In practice the generator uses the non-saturating version instead: $\max_G \mathbb{E}\big[\log D(G(z))\big]$

complexity.train: $O(P_G + P_D)$ per iteration
complexity.infer: Sampling takes a single generator forward pass; real-time capable

pros: Fast sampling with a single forward pass
use: Distillation to speed up diffusion models (adversarial loss)
cons: Unstable training
Mode collapse (generates only a few kinds of samples)
No likelihood available for evaluation
Replaced by diffusion models as the mainstream approach to text-to-image
hp: TTUR: a larger learning rate for the discriminator; Adam β₁ = 0.0–0.5
Spectral normalization, gradient penalty (WGAN-GP λ = 10), R1

leaves.name: StyleGAN
leaves.plain: An upgraded GAN that injects "style" layer by layer: coarse layers control face shape and pose, middle layers control facial features, and fine layers control strands of hair and skin texture. As a result it can generate ultra-realistic faces and precisely adjust features at a specific level.
leaves.intuition: A mapping network first turns the noise z into a more disentangled intermediate latent w, which then injects "style" at every resolution of the generator through adaptive normalization (AdaIN; replaced by weight modulation from v2 onward): coarse layers control pose and shape, fine layers control texture and color. It generates photorealistic faces and supports semantic editing.
leaves.objective:
$w = f(z)$ (8-layer MLP mapping network)
$\operatorname{AdaIN}(x_i, y) = y_{s,i} \cdot \frac{x_i - \mu(x_i)}{\sigma(x_i)} + y_{b,i}$, $y = A(w)$
Adversarial loss (non-saturating) + $R_1$ regularization + path length regularization (v2)

complexity.train: Very expensive ($1024^2$ resolution takes hundreds of GPU-days)

pros: Extremely high image quality within a single domain
Latent space supports semantic editing (GAN inversion)
use: High-resolution generation within a single domain, such as faces or products
cons: Can only generate a single domain
Diversity and text-conditioned control lag behind diffusion models
Expensive to train
hp: 0.5–0.8: trades diversity for quality at sampling time

children.name: Energy / Diffusion / Score Models
children.philosophy: Learns the energy function of the data distribution or its gradient (the score ∇ log p(x)), then goes from noise back to data via iterative denoising or Langevin dynamics.

leaves.name: Energy-Based Model (EBM)
leaves.plain: Instead of producing data directly, it gives every possible data point an "energy score": the more plausible and realistic, the lower the energy. Learning means pushing the energy of real data down and the energy of implausible data up. The framework is very general, but sampling and training are harder.
leaves.intuition: Rather than outputting probabilities directly, it learns an energy function E(x) that is low on real data and high everywhere else, with p(x) ∝ exp(−E(x)). The normalizing constant Z cannot be computed, so training "pushes energy down where the data is and up where the model samples", and sampling uses MCMC (e.g. Langevin dynamics). Diffusion and score-based models can be seen as successors that learn the gradient of the energy (the score).
leaves.objective:
$p_{	heta}(x) =  rac{\exp(-E_{	heta}(x))}{Z(	heta)}$
$
abla_{	heta} \log p(x) = -
abla_{	heta} E_{	heta}(x) + \mathbb{E}_{x' \sim p_{	heta}} ig[
abla_{	heta} E_{	heta}(x') ig]$ (the second term is approximated with contrastive divergence)
Langevin: $x_{t+1} = x_t -  rac{\eta}{2} 
abla_x E(x_t) + \sqrt{\eta} \cdot \epsilon$

complexity.train: $O(\text{MCMC steps} \cdot P)$ per iteration
complexity.infer: Sampling is $O(\text{MCMC steps} \cdot P)$, which is relatively slow

pros: The most flexible formulation: any network can serve as the energy function
Composable: adding energies acts as an AND of concepts
Can be used for anomaly detection and classification
use: Restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) recommender systems (historical use)
cons: Unstable training
Slow MCMC sampling with poor chain mixing
Intractable partition function, so no exact likelihood

leaves.name: DDPM
leaves.plain: First learn "how an image turns into pure noise when noise is added step by step", then train a model to learn the reverse: start from pure noise, remove the noise step by step, and finally "sculpt" a clear image. It delivers high quality with stable training and is the foundation of modern AI image generation.
leaves.intuition: The forward process adds Gaussian noise to the data bit by bit until only pure noise remains (fixed, with no parameters); a network then learns to reverse it: given xₜ and time t, predict the noise ε that was added. Generation starts from pure noise and denoises step by step. At its core, it learns the score ∇ log p(x) of the data distribution at every noise level.
leaves.objective:
Forward: $q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) I\big)$
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon} \big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_{\theta}(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2$
where $x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon$

complexity.train: $O(P)$ per iteration: sample one random $t$; stable training
complexity.infer: $O(T P)$, with $T = 1000$ steps originally; DDIM and DPM-Solver bring this down to 10–50 steps

pros: Combines sample quality and diversity, with no mode collapse
Easy to add conditional control (classifier-free guidance)
cons: Sampling needs many iterative steps, so it is slow
High resolution is costly in pixel space (which led to latent diffusion)
hp: Total number of steps in training

leaves.name: Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion)
leaves.plain: Running a diffusion model directly on pixels is too slow. Stable Diffusion first compresses the image into a much smaller "latent space", removes the noise there, and finally decompresses the result back into an image, with a text prompt guiding the generation. This slashes compute costs, so even an ordinary graphics card can generate images.
leaves.intuition: Pixel space is huge and full of perceptually unimportant detail. A VAE first compresses the image into a latent space that is 8× smaller in both height and width, and diffusion then runs in that latent space; text conditioning is injected into the U-Net via cross-attention. This cuts compute by an order of magnitude, making high-resolution text-to-image generation feasible on consumer GPUs.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{LDM}} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{E}(x), y, \epsilon, t} \big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_{\theta}\big(z_t, t, \tau_{\theta}(y)\big) \big\rVert^2$
$z = \mathcal{E}(x)$ is the VAE encoding; $\tau_{\theta}(y)$ is the output of the text encoder (CLIP, T5), injected via cross-attention
Classifier-free guidance: $\tilde{\epsilon} = \epsilon(z_t, \varnothing) + s \cdot \big( \epsilon(z_t, y) - \epsilon(z_t, \varnothing) \big)$

complexity.train: Same as DDPM, but carried out in an $(H/8) \times (W/8)$ latent space, which cuts FLOPs dramatically

pros: Rich ecosystem for conditional control (ControlNet, LoRA fine-tuning)
cons: VAE compression distorts fine details (text, fingers)
Multi-step sampling still takes time
Data copyright and bias concerns

leaves.name: DiT
leaves.plain: Swap the U-Net that does the denoising inside a diffusion model for a Transformer. The payoff is that bigger models keep getting better, so it scales very well; it is the mainstream architecture behind video generators such as Sora and the latest generation of image models.
leaves.intuition: Replace the diffusion model's U-Net backbone with a Transformer: the latent image is cut into patches that serve as tokens, and the timestep and conditioning modulate every layer through adaLN-Zero (initialized to the identity mapping for more stable training). Transformer scaling laws carry over to diffusion: the higher the GFLOPs, the lower the FID. It has become the mainstream backbone for image and video models such as Sora, SD3 and Flux.
leaves.objective:
Same objective as latent diffusion: $\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_{\theta}(z_t, t, c) \rVert^2$ (or the flow-matching velocity target instead)
adaLN-Zero: $\gamma, \beta, \alpha = \mathrm{MLP}(t_{\text{emb}} + c_{\text{emb}})$
$x \leftarrow x + \alpha \odot \operatorname{Attn}\big(\gamma \odot \mathrm{LN}(x) + \beta\big)$, with $\alpha$ initialized to 0

complexity.train: $O(N^2 d + N d^2)$ per layer per step, $N = (H/p)(W/p)$; for video, multiply by the temporal length

pros: Highly scalable, with predictable gains from scale
Easily handles multimodal and spatiotemporal video tokens
cons: Cost is quadratic in the number of tokens, making high resolutions and long videos very expensive
Requires large amounts of data and compute
Patch size is a trade-off between quality and cost
hp: How the spatiotemporal attention is factorized

children.name: Flow Models
children.philosophy: Uses invertible mappings or continuous velocity fields to "transport" a simple distribution into the data distribution; the former gives exact likelihoods, while the latter samples by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE).

leaves.name: Normalizing Flows (RealNVP / Glow)
leaves.plain: A chain of perfectly reversible transformations gradually warps a simple bell-shaped distribution into the complex distribution of the data. Because every step can be undone, the model can compute the exact probability of any sample and can also generate new samples directly from noise.
leaves.intuition: A sequence of invertible transformations with cheap-to-compute Jacobian determinants exactly "morphs" a simple distribution (a Gaussian) into the data distribution. Invertibility gives both exact likelihood evaluation and sampling. An affine coupling layer leaves half of the dimensions unchanged and uses them to compute the scale and shift for the other half, so the determinant is simply the product of the scale terms.
leaves.objective:
$\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z(f(x)) + \log \left| \det \frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x} \right|$
Affine coupling: $y_1 = x_1$, $y_2 = x_2 \odot \exp(s(x_1)) + t(x_1)$
$\Rightarrow \log \lvert \det J \rvert = \sum s(x_1)$

complexity.train: $O(K P)$ ($K$ = number of transformation layers), a single forward pass
complexity.infer: Both sampling and likelihood evaluation take a single forward pass
complexity.space: $O(P)$; the latent dimension must equal the data dimension

cons: Invertibility limits expressiveness, so very deep networks are needed
Image quality falls short of diffusion models and GANs
The latent dimension must equal the data dimension, so no compression is possible
hp: Size of the s / t networks
Factor out some dimensions at each level

leaves.name: Flow Matching / Rectified Flow
leaves.zh: Flow matching / rectified flow (simulation-free generative flows)
leaves.plain: The model directly learns a path that "flows" from noise to real data, keeping it as straight as possible. The straighter the path, the fewer steps generation needs, so it is faster and simpler than classic diffusion models, and many new-generation image and video models have adopted it.
leaves.intuition: Instead of simulating a noising process, it directly learns a "velocity field" that pushes noise points along a path to data points. The simplest path is a straight line xₜ = (1 − t)·x₀ + t·x₁ (x₀ is noise, x₁ is data), so the target velocity is simply x₁ − x₀ and training reduces to a plain regression. Straight paths sharply reduce the number of steps ODE sampling needs; both SD3 and Flux use this objective.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, x_1} \big\lVert v_{\theta}(x_t, t) - (x_1 - x_0) \big\rVert^2$
$t \sim U[0,1],\ x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),\ x_1 \sim p_{\text{data}}$
$x_t = (1 - t) x_0 + t x_1$
Sampling: solve the ODE $\frac{dx}{dt} = v_{\theta}(x, t)$

complexity.train: $O(P)$ per iteration; simulation-free, as cheap as diffusion
complexity.infer: $O(\text{steps} \cdot P)$, typically 10–30 steps; reflow or distillation can bring this down to 1–4 steps

pros: Theoretically unifies diffusion and flow models
cons: Still requires multi-step ODE solving
Details such as the timestep sampling distribution (e.g. logit-normal) affect quality
A newer method; best practices are still evolving
hp: ODE solver and number of steps

children.name: Reinforcement Learning
children.signal: Rewards (usually delayed) obtained by interacting with an environment: nobody tells the model the correct action, there is only feedback on "how well it did", and the model has to balance exploration and exploitation on its own.
children.criterion: L2 split criterion: whether actions change the environment's future state (single-step vs. sequential decisions)

children.name: Single-Step Decisions (Multi-Armed / Contextual Bandits)
children.def: Each round, choose one action and immediately receive a reward; actions do not change future states, so the only difficulty is the trade-off between exploration (trying uncertain options) and exploitation (choosing the currently best option).
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: exploration mechanism (random perturbation / optimistic upper confidence bounds / posterior sampling)

children.name: Random Exploration
children.philosophy: Picks at random with a fixed or decaying probability, without considering the uncertainty of each action.

leaves.name: ε-Greedy
leaves.plain: Most of the time, pick the option that currently looks best (exploitation), but spend a small fraction of the time (ε, e.g. 10%) trying options at random (exploration) so you don't miss a better one. It is the simplest exploration strategy there is.
leaves.intuition: The most naive way to trade off exploration and exploitation: with probability 1 − ε take the action with the best current estimate, and with probability ε pick an action at random. Simple, but the exploration is "blind": actions already known to be poor keep getting tried again and again.
leaves.objective:
$a_t = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a} \hat{Q}(a)$ (with probability $1 - \epsilon$), otherwise uniformly at random
Incremental mean: $\hat{Q}(a) \leftarrow \hat{Q}(a) + \frac{r - \hat{Q}(a)}{N(a)}$
With a suitably decaying $\epsilon$, cumulative regret can reach $O(\log T)$

complexity.train: $O(K)$ per step

use: Baseline for exploration in recommender systems
Exploration strategy for RL algorithms such as DQN
cons: With a fixed ε, cumulative regret grows linearly
Ignores uncertainty when exploring
The ε decay schedule needs tuning

children.name: Optimistic Confidence Bounds
children.philosophy: Optimism in the face of uncertainty: each action's score = estimated value + uncertainty bonus, which gives exploration a direction.

leaves.name: UCB1
leaves.plain: "Be optimistic about what you're unsure of": each option's score = its average performance so far + a bonus that grows the less the option has been tried. Rarely tried options naturally get a chance, and once they have been tried enough the bonus fades away.
leaves.intuition: Each action's score = average reward + an uncertainty bonus; the fewer times it has been tried, the larger the bonus. Exploration therefore becomes directed: only actions that "could still be the best" get explored. In theory, cumulative regret is O(log T).
leaves.objective:
$a_t = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a} \left[ \hat{Q}(a) + c \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2 \ln t}{N(a)}} \right]$ (UCB1 uses $c = 1$; rewards must lie in $[0, 1]$)
Cumulative regret $= O\left( \sum_{a:\, \Delta_a > 0} \frac{\ln T}{\Delta_a} \right)$

complexity.train: $O(K)$ per step

use: UCT in Monte Carlo tree search
cons: Assumes bounded, stationary rewards
Non-stationary settings need sliding-window or discounted variants
In practice often over-explores compared with Thompson Sampling
hp: Tune the window size or discount factor

leaves.name: LinUCB
leaves.plain: A "know your audience" version of UCB: it predicts how well each option will do given the context (user features, time of day), then adds an uncertainty bonus before choosing. Commonly used for personalized recommendations and news placements.
leaves.intuition: Brings user or context features into the picture: the expected reward is assumed to be a linear function of the context features, E[r | x, a] = xₐᵀθₐ. θ is estimated with ridge regression, and the width of the confidence ellipsoid, √(xᵀA⁻¹x), serves as the uncertainty bonus. For users with a feature combination it has never seen, it automatically explores more.
leaves.objective:
$A_a = D_a^\top D_a + I$, $b_a = D_a^\top c_a$, $\hat{\theta}_a = A_a^{-1} b_a$
$p_{t,a} = x_{t,a}^\top \hat{\theta}_a + \alpha \cdot \sqrt{x_{t,a}^\top A_a^{-1} x_{t,a}}$
Choose $\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a} p_{t,a}$

complexity.train: $O(K \cdot d^2)$ per step (updating $A^{-1}$ with Sherman-Morrison)

use: News and content recommendation (Yahoo! front-page experiment)
cons: Requires the linearity assumption
The d² cost is high when the feature dimension is large
Depends on good feature engineering
hp: Initial value of A is λI

children.name: Posterior Sampling
children.philosophy: Maintains a Bayesian posterior over each action's reward, and chooses actions according to "the posterior probability that it is the optimal action".

leaves.name: Thompson Sampling
leaves.plain: Keep a probability distribution for each option that captures "how good I think it is"; each round, draw one number from each distribution and pick the option with the highest draw. More uncertain options occasionally draw a very high number and get tried, so exploration and exploitation balance out naturally. In practice it is often the best performer.
leaves.intuition: Maintain a Bayesian posterior over each action's reward; each round, draw one sample from each posterior and take the action with the largest sampled value. The probability that an action is chosen equals exactly the posterior probability that it is the optimal action (probability matching), so uncertainty translates naturally into exploration.
leaves.objective:
Bernoulli rewards: $\theta_a \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_a, \beta_a)$
Each round, draw $\tilde{\theta}_a \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_a, \beta_a)$ and choose $\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a} \tilde{\theta}_a$
After observing reward $r$, update: $\alpha_a \leftarrow \alpha_a + r$, $\beta_a \leftarrow \beta_a + 1 - r$

complexity.train: $O(K)$ per step (conjugate case)

pros: Extends to contextual settings (linear TS, neural TS)
A forgetting mechanism can be added for non-stationary settings
use: Dynamic traffic allocation in online A/B/n experiments
cons: Non-conjugate models need approximate posteriors (MCMC, variational, bootstrap)
Randomness makes results harder to reproduce
The choice of prior affects early behavior
hp: Beta(1, 1) uninformative prior, or set from historical data
Discount factor γ or a sliding window
In practice the posterior is often updated in batches

children.name: Sequential Decisions (Markov Decision Processes)
children.def: Actions change the environment's state and affect future rewards, so credit must be assigned across time: which step should get credit for this reward? The goal is to maximize the discounted cumulative return $\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_t \gamma^t r_t\big]$.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: how actions are determined (implicitly by a value function / output directly by a parameterized policy / planned with a model of the environment); any method that uses an environment model for planning or imagination is always classified as model-based

children.name: Value-Based
children.philosophy: Learns the state-action value $Q(s, a)$, with the policy given implicitly by $\operatorname*{arg\,max}_a Q(s, a)$; updates by bootstrapping through the Bellman equation.

leaves.name: Q-Learning
leaves.plain: While playing, it learns a table of "how many points will I score in the long run if I take this action in this state." After each move, it corrects the table using "the reward just received + the best expected outcome from the next step." Even if its behavior while learning is quite random, it still ends up learning the best strategy.
leaves.intuition: Learns the long-run value Q(s, a) of every state–action pair by bootstrapping with the Bellman optimality equation: the current estimate is updated toward the target "immediate reward + the best Q-value in the next state." It is an off-policy method: behavior can explore freely, yet what it learns is the value of the optimal policy.
leaves.objective:
$Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a)$
$\quad + \alpha \big[ r + \gamma \cdot \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \big]$
Optimal policy: $\pi^*(s) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a} Q^*(s, a)$

complexity.train: $O(\lvert A \rvert)$ per update (tabular)

pros: Convergence guarantee in the tabular case with sufficient exploration and a suitable learning rate
Off-policy, so experience can be reused
use: Inventory and scheduling decisions that can be discretized
cons: Tables become infeasible for large state spaces
The max operator causes overestimation bias (Double Q-learning corrects it)
Not applicable to continuous actions

leaves.name: DQN
leaves.plain: When there are too many states (e.g., game screens), Q-Learning's table can't hold them all, so DQN uses a neural network to estimate the values instead. Two tricks, "experience replay" and a "target network," keep training stable, and for the first time an AI learned to play Atari games just by looking at the screen.
leaves.intuition: Approximates the Q-function with a deep network, and was the first to learn Atari games directly from pixels. Two keys to stable training: experience replay (breaks correlations between samples and reuses data) and a target network (weights copied periodically so the TD target stays fixed for a while). Later improvements such as Double DQN, Dueling, and Prioritized Replay were combined into Rainbow.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s, a, r, s') \sim \mathcal{D}} \Big[ \big( r + \gamma \cdot \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-)$
$\qquad - Q(s, a; \theta) \big)^2 \Big]$ (Huber loss is often used instead)
Target network: every $C$ steps, set $\theta^- \leftarrow \theta$

complexity.train: $O(B \cdot P)$ per gradient step

pros: Handles high-dimensional observations such as images
Reuses experience; more sample-efficient than pure policy gradients
cons: Discrete actions only
Prone to overestimation bias and unstable training
Sensitive to hyperparameters

leaves.name: CQL
leaves.plain: When a model can only learn from previously collected data and can no longer try things out in the environment (offline reinforcement learning), it tends to overestimate actions it has never seen. CQL deliberately gives "conservative ratings" to actions that never appear in the data, so it avoids learning risky strategies that only look good on paper.
