leaves.intuition: Offline reinforcement learning can only use existing historical logs and cannot interact with the environment again. The problem is that the Q-network often badly overestimates actions that never appear in the data, and the policy then chases these illusory high values. CQL adds an extra term to the loss that pushes down the Q-values of all actions and pushes up the Q-values of actions actually present in the data. The learned Q is a lower bound on the true value, so the policy stays conservatively within the data's coverage.
leaves.objective:
$\min_{Q}\ \alpha \cdot \Bigg( \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \log \sum_{a} \exp Q(s, a) \right]$
$\qquad - \mathbb{E}_{(s, a) \sim \mathcal{D}} \big[ Q(s, a) \big] \Bigg)$
$\quad + \tfrac12 \cdot \mathbb{E}_{(s, a, s') \sim \mathcal{D}} \Big[ \big( Q(s, a) - \hat{\mathcal{B}}^{\pi} \hat{Q}(s, a) \big)^2 \Big]$

complexity.train: Same as SAC or DQN, plus a logsumexp over sampled actions

pros: Can learn a policy directly from historical logs
use: Learning from historical recommendation or ad logs
Industrial control where trial and error is not an option
cons: Can be overly conservative and fail to learn a policy better than the data
α needs tuning
Evaluating an offline policy is itself hard (OPE)
hp: Degree of conservatism; can also be tuned automatically with a Lagrangian method

children.name: Policy-Based (Policy Gradient / Actor-Critic)
children.philosophy: Parameterizes the policy $\pi_\theta(a \mid s)$ directly and updates it along the gradient of the expected return; a value network (critic) can serve as a baseline to reduce variance.

leaves.name: REINFORCE
leaves.plain: The most direct way to learn a strategy: after playing a full round, actions that led to good results become more likely next time, and those that led to bad results become less likely. The idea is simple, but because you have to wait until the round is over to know how things went, the learning signal is noisy and learning is less efficient.
leaves.intuition: Performs gradient ascent directly on the policy parameters: raise the probability of actions with good outcomes and lower it for bad ones. The policy gradient theorem means we don't need to know the environment dynamics; sampled trajectories and their returns are enough to estimate the gradient. Subtracting a baseline b(s) reduces variance without introducing bias.
leaves.objective:
$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta} \Bigg[ \sum_{t} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)$
$\qquad \cdot \big( G_t - b(s_t) \big) \Bigg]$
$G_t = \sum_{k \ge t} \gamma^{k - t} \cdot r_k$

complexity.train: $O(T \cdot P)$ per trajectory

pros: Works for both continuous and discrete actions
use: RL fine-tuning of sequence generation models (e.g. RLOO)
cons: Very high gradient variance
Poor sample efficiency
On-policy; cannot reuse old data
hp: Average return or a value network

leaves.name: PPO
leaves.plain: During policy learning it limits how much each update can change things, so one big change can't make performance collapse. Stable, easy to tune, and effective, it is the most widely used algorithm for robot control and for the human-feedback training (RLHF) of early ChatGPT.
leaves.intuition: If a policy-gradient step is too large, the policy collapses. PPO measures how far the new policy has moved from the old one with the importance ratio $r_t = \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{old}}$ and clips it to $[1 - \epsilon,\ 1 + \epsilon]$: improvement beyond that range earns no further reward. It is a first-order simplification of TRPO's trust region; stable and simple, it became the default algorithm for RLHF.
leaves.objective:
$L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \Big[ \min\big( r_t(\theta) \cdot \hat{A}_t,$
$\qquad \operatorname{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon) \cdot \hat{A}_t \big) \Big]$
$r_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}$; $\hat{A}_t$ is estimated with $\text{GAE}(\lambda)$
The total loss also includes a value-function error term and an entropy bonus; RLHF further adds $-\beta \cdot \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \parallel \pi_{\text{ref}})$

complexity.train: $O(K_{\text{epochs}} \cdot N_{\text{samples}} \cdot P)$ per iteration
complexity.space: rollout buffer + actor / critic (RLHF must hold four models in memory at once: policy, reference, reward, and value)

pros: Works for both continuous and discrete actions
use: RLHF alignment of large language models
cons: On-policy, so less sample-efficient
Implementation details (normalization, value clipping) matter a lot
Large memory overhead in RLHF
hp: About 3e-4 for control tasks; on the order of 1e-6 for LLMs
Exploration and how far the policy may drift from the reference model

leaves.name: SAC
leaves.plain: Besides chasing high rewards, it encourages behavior to stay somewhat random while learning (don't decide too early that there is only one way to do things). It explores more thoroughly, trains more stably, and learns from fewer samples, which makes it well suited to continuous-control tasks such as robotic arms.
leaves.intuition: Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning: besides reward, the objective also asks the policy to be "as random as possible" (high entropy), which naturally encourages exploration, makes it more robust to disturbances, and keeps it from converging prematurely to a single action. It is off-policy and takes the minimum of two Q-networks to curb overestimation, making it one of the most sample-efficient methods for continuous control.
leaves.objective:
$J(\pi) = \sum_{t} \mathbb{E}\big[ r(s_t, a_t) + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot \mid s_t)) \big]$
$Q$ target:
$y = r + \gamma \big( \min_{i=1,2} Q_{\bar{\theta}_i}(s', \tilde{a}')$
$\qquad - \alpha \log \pi(\tilde{a}' \mid s') \big)$
Policy: $\min \mathbb{E}\big[ \alpha \cdot \log \pi(a \mid s) - \min_{i} Q_{\theta_i}(s, a) \big]$ (reparameterized); $\alpha$ can be tuned automatically toward a target entropy

complexity.train: $O(B \cdot P)$ per gradient step (actor + two critics + target networks)

pros: Automatic temperature tuning makes it insensitive to hyperparameters
cons: Designed mainly for continuous actions; discrete actions need a modified version
The replay buffer takes up memory
Multiple networks add compute

leaves.name: DPO
leaves.plain: To make a language model match human preferences, you don't need to first train a separate scoring model and then run reinforcement learning; instead, you tune the model directly on paired data saying "this answer is better than that one." The process is simpler and more stable, and the results come close to RLHF.
leaves.intuition: RLHF first trains a reward model and then optimizes with PPO, which makes for a complex pipeline. DPO observes that in the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem, the optimal policy and the reward have a closed-form relationship: $r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \text{const}$. Substituting this into the Bradley-Terry preference model lets you train the policy directly on preference pairs with a classification loss, with no reward model and no sampling.
leaves.objective:
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)} \bigg[ \log \sigma\bigg( \beta \cdot \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}$
$\qquad - \beta \cdot \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} \bigg) \bigg]$
($y_w$ is the preferred response, $y_l$ the dispreferred one)

complexity.train: Each pair needs two forward passes through the policy and two through the reference model

pros: Simple and stable; as easy to train as supervised fine-tuning
Removes the reward model and the RL loop
use: Preference alignment of large language models
cons: Offline method: uses only fixed preference data, with no online exploration
Prone to over-optimization and overfitting the preference data
Performance degrades under distribution shift
hp: 0.1–0.5; smaller values allow more drift from the reference model
leaves.note: DPO does not interact with an environment, but its derivation starts from a KL-regularized RL objective and what it outputs is a policy, so it is classified as policy-based; strictly speaking, it "solves an RL objective with a supervised loss."

leaves.name: GRPO
leaves.plain: The model produces a group of answers to the same question, and the answers are compared with one another: those better than the group average are reinforced and worse ones are weakened. No separate scoring network is needed, which saves memory, and it is a key method for training reasoning models (such as DeepSeek-R1).
leaves.intuition: PPO needs a value network as large as the policy to estimate advantages, which is expensive. GRPO samples a group of G responses to the same prompt and uses the standardized within-group rewards as the advantages (the within-group comparison acts as the baseline), eliminating the value network. Combined with verifiable rewards (whether a math answer is right, whether code passes its tests), it trains long-chain reasoning ability (DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1).
leaves.objective:
$\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}$
$J = \mathbb{E}\Bigg[ \frac{1}{G} \sum_{i} \frac{1}{\lvert o_i \rvert} \sum_{t} \min\big( \rho_{i,t} \cdot \hat{A}_i,$
$\qquad \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t}, 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon) \cdot \hat{A}_i \big)$
$\qquad - \beta \cdot D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta \parallel \pi_{\text{ref}}) \Bigg]$
$\rho = \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{old}}$

complexity.train: Each prompt requires generating $G$ responses, $O(G \cdot L \cdot P)$; generation is the dominant cost
complexity.space: No critic needed, saving roughly half the memory

pros: Well suited to tasks with verifiable rewards
use: Training math and coding reasoning models
Alignment on tasks with clear right/wrong criteria
cons: Requires heavy sampling, so generation is expensive
No gradient when rewards are sparse or the whole group gets the same score
Details such as length bias need fixing (e.g. variants like Dr. GRPO)
hp: Caps the length of the reasoning chain

children.name: Model-Based
children.philosophy: Uses a known or learned model of the environment's dynamics to plan ahead or imagine "in its head", reducing real interaction.

leaves.name: MCTS / AlphaZero
leaves.plain: Like a player thinking "if I move here and my opponent replies there...", it simulates ahead in its head, but a neural network judges which moves deserve a closer look and who has the upper hand, so only promising branches get explored in depth. It learns entirely through self-play and has surpassed humans at Go and chess.
leaves.intuition: When the rules are known (a simulator is available), decisions can be made by "thinking ahead": Monte Carlo tree search repeatedly performs selection, expansion, evaluation, and backup, using PUCT to balance exploration and exploitation. AlphaZero replaces random rollouts with a single neural network that outputs both a policy prior and a value, then trains that network through self-play with the search results as supervised targets. Search improves the policy, and the policy in turn speeds up the search.
leaves.objective:
Selection: $a = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a} \Big[ Q(s, a)$
$\qquad + c_{\text{puct}} \cdot P(s, a) \cdot \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1 + N(s, a)} \Big]$
Network loss: $l = (z - v)^2 - \pi^\top \log p + c \lVert \theta \rVert^2$ ($z$ is the game outcome, $\pi$ the visit-count distribution from search)

complexity.train: Self-play requires massive compute
complexity.infer: $O(N_{\text{sim}} \cdot P)$ per move, where $N_{\text{sim}}$ is the number of simulations (e.g. 800)

pros: Superhuman play in Go, chess, and shogi
use: Combinatorial optimization (chip placement, matrix multiplication in AlphaTensor)
Scheduling problems that need lookahead planning
cons: Requires a perfect simulator
Enormous computational cost
Stochastic or partially observable environments require modifications
hp: Exploration at the root node (α = 0.3 for chess)
Sample by visit counts for the first few moves
How much self-play data is retained

leaves.name: MuZero
leaves.zh: Planning with a learned latent model
leaves.plain: You don't even have to tell it the rules of the game. It learns its own "mental simulator" that predicts only what matters for decisions (rewards, how good a position is, what move to make), then plans inside that simulator. The same method works for both Go and Atari.
leaves.intuition: Planning without knowing the rules: learn a "latent model" that predicts only the three things planning needs (reward, value, policy) rather than reconstructing the observations themselves, then run MCTS in this learned latent space. It reaches state-of-the-art performance on both Atari and board games.
leaves.objective:
Representation function $h$: $s^0 = h(o_1, \ldots, o_t)$
Dynamics function $g$: $(r^k, s^k) = g(s^{k-1}, a^k)$
Prediction function $f$: $(p^k, v^k) = f(s^k)$
$l = \sum_{k=0}^{K} \Big[ l^r(u_{t+k}, r^k) + l^v(z_{t+k}, v^k)$
$\qquad + l^p(\pi_{t+k}, p^k) \Big] + c \lVert \theta \rVert^2$

complexity.train: Very expensive

pros: No knowledge of the environment's rules required
Good sample efficiency (extended further by EfficientZero)
use: Sequential decision-making where the rules are unknown or hard to model
Video compression (a real-world case: YouTube VP9 bitrate control)
cons: Complex to implement and train
High compute requirements
Stochastic environments require Stochastic MuZero
hp: Recompute targets for old data with the latest model

leaves.name: DreamerV3
leaves.plain: It first learns a "world model" that predicts how the environment will change, then practices extensively in its own "imagination," cutting down on real-world trial and error. A single set of settings performs well across many different tasks, including finding diamonds in Minecraft on its own.
leaves.intuition: First learn a world model (a recurrent state-space model, RSSM, that compresses observations into latent states and predicts the next step and the reward), then roll out latent trajectories "in imagination" to train an actor-critic, greatly reducing real interaction. v3 uses the symlog transform and a single fixed set of hyperparameters across more than 150 tasks, and was the first to collect diamonds in Minecraft without any human data (Nature, 2025).
leaves.objective:
World model: $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}$
$\quad + \beta_{\text{dyn}} \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}} + \beta_{\text{rep}} \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}}$
($\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}$: reconstructs observations, rewards, and continue flags; the last two terms are KL balancing with free bits)
Actor: maximizes the $\lambda$-return of imagined trajectories (with entropy regularization)
Critic: predicts the $\lambda$-return via symlog discrete regression

complexity.train: World model $O(B \cdot T \cdot P_{\text{wm}})$ + imagination rollouts $O(B \cdot H \cdot P)$

pros: One set of hyperparameters works across domains
Handles image inputs and sparse rewards
use: Control problems where real interaction is costly
cons: World-model errors get amplified in imagination (model bias)
Complex architecture
Long-horizon planning ability is still limited
hp: Amount of training per step of real interaction
v3 is designed to need no tuning
